title: Richard Branson’s wife could have survived with crucial medication, coroner finds
summary: A British coroner found Lady Joan Branson's fatal pulmonary embolism could have been prevented with blood thinners after her fall on Necker Island.
story: NASCAR driver Kyle Busch, 41, died from severe pneumonia that escalated into sepsis, his family confirmed. Dr. Cedric Rutland, a pulmonary critical care physician and American Lung Association spokesperson, explains how pneumonia's inflammation and infection can overwhelm the body.
The death of Richard Branson's wife, Lady Joan Branson, could have been prevented if she had received medication to prevent blood clots, a British coroner reportedly found.
Lady Branson died at the age of 80 after being admitted to a hospital in November 2025 after a fall weeks earlier on Necker Island, a British Virgin Island owned by her billionaire husband.
Her cause of death was determined to be a pulmonary embolism caused by deep vein thrombosis (DVT), in which a blood clot travels to the lungs and blocks an artery, the BBC reported.
KIM KARDASHIAN REVEALS NEW HEALTH SCARE WITH HAUNTING CONNECTION TO FATHER'S CANCER DEATH

Senior Coroner Fiona Wilcox told Westminster Coroner's Court earlier this month that Lady Branson did not receive preventive anticoagulants, commonly known as blood thinners, at the hospital despite a "very high risk of developing deep vein thrombosis," according to the outlet.
A British coroner concluded Lady Joan Branson's death likely could have been prevented with preventive blood-thinning medication. (Axelle/Bauer-Griffin/FilmMagic)
According to testimony during the legal inquest, Lady Branson's biggest risk factors included her immobility after a fracture following her fall.
"I do find her death would have likely been prevented, and the lack of anticoagulation did cause or contribute to her death probably," Wilcox said.
COMMON ANTIBIOTIC LINKED TO HIGHER RISK OF DEATH IN ADULTS, MAJOR STUDY FINDS
Wilcox added, however, that the case was not one of neglect because Branson did receive medical care.
The inquest, she said, was to "explore the facts, come to the correct conclusions and learn lessons from this," The Independent reported.
The inquest into Lady Joan Branson's death has drawn attention to the importance of preventing dangerous blood clots in hospitalized patients. (Tim Graham/Sygma/Corbis via Getty Images))

During the inquest, doctors gave differing testimony about whether bleeding risk justified withholding the medication, namely enoxaparin, an injectable blood thinner commonly used to help prevent blood clots in hospitalized patients.
EVERYDAY HABIT LINKED TO DRAMATICALLY LOWER RISK OF DYING FROM HEART DISEASE
The hospital's admitting doctor, Dr. Basir Kunduzi, testified he did not complete a bleeding risk assessment on the day of Lady Branson's admission.
Kunduzi said Lady Branson's death led him to "reflect on [his] role as a doctor" and the importance of "good communication between team members," according to the BBC.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Fox News Digital has reached out to the hospital for comment.
The case highlights the importance of balancing blood clot prevention with bleeding risk when treating hospitalized patients. (iStock)

The findings highlight the lifesaving role of blood thinners, which are often used in hospitals to help prevent DVT in patients who are unable to move normally after surgery, fractures or prolonged bed rest. They can increase the risk of bleeding, however, so doctors must weigh both risks before giving them.

Nearly all hospitalized adults should receive some form of blood clot prevention, either with blood-thinning medication or mechanical devices that help keep blood flowing in the legs, Dr. Jared Ross, a South Carolina-based emergency medicine physician, told Fox News Digital.
"In the vast majority of cases, the benefits outweigh the risks," Ross, who was not involved in the inquest or Branson's care, added.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER
A spokeswoman for Sir Branson said the family does not plan to comment on the inquest and pointed to the numerous social media posts he has made for his wife.
Sir Richard Branson paid tribute to his wife after her death, calling her the "shining star" of their family. (Patrick T. Fallon/AFP via Getty Images)

"Life will never be the same without her," Branson wrote on Instagram last year, calling her the "shining star" of the family. "But we have fifty incredible years of memories — years filled with tears and laughter, kindness, and a love that shaped our family more than words could ever capture. It was a relationship that worked. We just had lots of laughs. We were very lucky."
CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS
Although pulmonary embolisms can be life-threatening, prompt treatment greatly improves the chances of survival, making early recognition critical.
Symptoms of DVT can include swelling, pain or tenderness, warmth and redness in the affected leg or arm, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

Richard Branson and Joan Templeman married on Necker Island in 1989, the same private Caribbean island where she suffered the fall that preceded her final hospitalization. (PA Images via Getty Images)

A pulmonary embolism, which occurs when a clot travels to the lungs, may cause shortness of breath, chest pain that worsens with deep breathing or coughing, a rapid or irregular heartbeat, coughing up blood, lightheadedness or fainting.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The CDC and the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute say anyone with symptoms of a pulmonary embolism should seek immediate medical attention.
Deirdre Bardolf is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital.

title: Tropical disease spread by mosquitoes claims first recorded death in southern US state
summary: Gay Small died on her 80th birthday from dengue after a mosquito bite near her Tampa home, the Florida Department of Health confirmed Friday.
story: Dr. Tyler Evans, an infectious diseases and addiction medicine doctor and associate professor at University of Southern California Keck School of Medicine, discusses the spread, symptoms and management of West Nile virus.
Florida recorded its first confirmed dengue fever death of 2026 earlier this month, according to the Florida Department of Health.

Gay Small of Hillsborough County died Sept. 4 — her 80th birthday — from complications of a dengue infection, including septic shock and multi-organ failure, after she was bitten by a mosquito near her home on Bayshore Boulevard, The Tampa Bay Times reported.

"Cheated. Just, you know, it’s so unfair because she was in good health, and she worked hard to stay healthy, and she walked, and she ate right and, you know, all the things that you’re supposed to do," Small's daughter, Anna Small, told Tampa's WFLA Channel 8.
DANGEROUS MOSQUITO-BORNE VIRUS SPREADS IN ONE STATE AS OFFICIALS WARN OF RISING CASES
"And, you know, this virus just kind of comes out of nowhere. She met the wrong mosquito, and that’s it," Anna Small said.
Small's family said they believe Gay Small first caught dengue years ago while traveling abroad but didn't know it. People who have had dengue before are much more likely to develop severe symptoms.

"While in the hospital, Small said, her mother was weak, her hands turned red and she had trembles that she could hear in her voice," WFLA reported. "She had to go into the ICU by the middle of the week."
A mosquito feeds on human skin. Dengue is spread to people through the bite of an infected mosquito and can cause fever, severe aches, nausea and rash. (iStock)
Small's late husband, Bob Small, spent his career working on dengue vaccines, according to the couple's daughter.
The Florida Department of Health confirmed the death Friday after completing its investigation but did not release additional information, WFLA reported.
The Times, citing University of South Florida public health instructor Kristi Miley, reported that a dengue death had not been recorded in the Tampa Bay area in nearly a century.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

Dengue is a mosquito-borne viral illness that can cause fever, severe aches, nausea, rash and, in rare cases, life-threatening complications, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

The virus is most prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions, including Southeast Asia, the Western Pacific islands, Latin America and Africa. Though less common in the continental U.S., locally acquired cases have been recorded in Florida, California and Texas.

Florida mosquito control agencies have stepped up surveillance, inspections and spraying, as locally acquired dengue fever cases — which means people contracted the illness where they live rather than while traveling abroad — have climbed in recent weeks.
Gay Small’s late husband, Bob Small, spent his career working on dengue vaccines — the same mosquito-borne disease that ultimately claimed his wife’s life, according to reports. (iStock)

The Times reported that, since July, Florida "has been experiencing an unprecedented outbreak of locally caught cases." Hillsborough County, where Small lived, "has been at the epicenter of the epidemic."
Hillsborough and Pinellas counties are under mosquito-borne illness alerts issued by the Florida Department of Health.
"Dengue does not stop at county lines," Pinellas County Mosquito Control Director Alissa Berro told Fox 13.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS
"The mosquitoes that transmit the virus generally stay within a relatively small area, but people travel throughout the Tampa Bay area every day," he said.

"When someone infected with dengue enters a new area, a local mosquito can bite that person and later spread the virus to others. As cases rise across the region, so does the potential for additional local transmission."

In addition to increasing aerial and ground treatments in areas showing dengue virus activity, Hillsborough County Mosquito Management Services has also been inspecting private properties for potential mosquito breeding sites, according to local reports.
Mosquito-control crews across the Tampa Bay area have increased surveillance and treatments as locally acquired dengue cases climb. (iStock)
The increased application of insecticide and larvicide by helicopters appears to be working, the Times reported.
"Of the last 1,500 mosquitoes they've sent for testing, all have returned negative for dengue," it said.

The Florida Mosquito Control Association (FMCA) is urging residents to empty or cover standing water around their homes. The mosquito that spreads dengue is a container breeder, meaning it lays eggs in buckets, planters, plant saucers, tires, discarded toys and other objects that collect small amounts of water, experts say.
The FMCA also advises people to follow what it calls the "three Ds."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Dress in long sleeves, light colors and closed-toed shoes outdoors.Defend with a repellent containing DEET, picaridin, IR3535 or oil of lemon eucalyptus.Dump standing water from containers around the home and check yards regularly.
Dress in long sleeves, light colors and closed-toed shoes outdoors.
Defend with a repellent containing DEET, picaridin, IR3535 or oil of lemon eucalyptus.
Dump standing water from containers around the home and check yards regularly.

Many people infected with dengue have no symptoms, and most people who do become sick recover within a week or two, according to the Mayo Clinic. In some cases, however, the illness can progress to severe dengue, a potentially life-threatening condition.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Warning signs can develop quickly, often within a day or two after a fever subsides. Those may include severe stomach pain, repeated vomiting, unusual bleeding or bruising, difficulty breathing, extreme tiredness and irritability or restlessness. People experiencing warning signs of severe dengue should seek immediate medical care.
Teresa Mull is a freelance writer with the Lifestyle team at Fox News Digital.

title: Women turn to testosterone for low sex drive as doctors confront treatment ‘experimentation’
summary: Dr. Kudzai Dombo reveals the insurance denials and dosing guesswork women face seeking testosterone therapy as FDA regulators weigh new access.
story: OB-GYN Kudzai Dombo shares why interest in testosterone is rising among women, what evidence says about libido,and why access, dosing and insurance coverage can be complicated.

When women ask their doctors about taking testosterone to help with menopause symptoms, they can run into insurance rejections, confusing workarounds and dosing guesswork since no testosterone product is FDA-approved for women in the U.S.
On Thursday, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) convened a public workshop to examine the evidence, safety and research gaps with testosterone therapy for menopausal women.

Interest in testosterone therapy has grown as more women seek treatment for symptoms such as low sexual desire, fatigue and reduced quality of life during menopause. Yet the lack of an FDA-approved product has left physicians relying on off-label prescribing and compounded formulations.
MELINDA FRENCH GATES SAYS IT TOOK 3 DOCTORS TO DIAGNOSE THE CONDITION SHE WAS SUFFERING FROM

Dr. Kudzai Dombo, a board-certified obstetrician-gynecologist, Menopause Society-certified practitioner and prescribing physician at Alloy Health, said she sees this dynamic playing out daily at her own Los Angeles practice.
Interest in testosterone therapy has grown as more women seek treatment for symptoms such as low sexual desire, fatigue and reduced quality of life during menopause, doctors say. (iStock)
Once patients get settled on standard estrogen and progesterone regimens, "the immediate next question is, do I need testosterone?" Dombo told Fox News Digital.

Although women may hear about a wide range of potential benefits on social media and from friends, current evidence-based guidelines support testosterone therapy for only one indication: hypoactive sexual desire disorder (HSDD), or persistently low sexual desire.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Clinical evidence supporting its use for energy, mood, bone health or sleep remains limited, though many patients are eager to try it for those secondary benefits, according to Dombo.
The absence of FDA-approved female testosterone products forces patients to rely on compounded creams, over-the-counter purchases abroad or micro-dosed male gels. (iStock)

Because no female-specific formulation exists, doctors must navigate off-label workarounds. They typically choose between using custom compounding pharmacies or micro-dosing FDA-approved male gel packets, which patients must carefully measure out at home.
ALZHEIMER'S RISK MAY BE 35% LOWER WITH COMMON MENOPAUSE TREATMENT, STUDY FINDS

This lack of standardized options creates administrative and financial hurdles. Because the therapy is off-label, insurance routinely denies coverage, forcing clinicians and patients to improvise, a frustration that Dombo experienced firsthand.

"When I was prescribed testosterone, my insurance denied coverage, and my physician recommended a compounded cream to avoid the administrative burden," Dombo recalled. "I said, 'Well, I've already tried compounded, and I actually want to try the gel.'"
"Sexual health is part of your entire health."
Using a discount coupon, she paid out of pocket and discovered that a 10-month supply of male gel packets was actually cheaper than a single month of compounded cream.
"It's just an example, I think, of how we have to adapt to a system that has not supported patients when it comes to access to testosterone therapy," she said.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Dosing male products can also present clinical challenges. Dombo described a patient in her private practice who precisely measured out one-tenth of a male gel packet daily using a syringe.
Despite three months of consistency, follow-up bloodwork showed no change in hormone levels, and the patient experienced no symptom relief.
Rising advocacy from patients and medical professionals has pushed federal regulators to officially evaluate standardized access and scientific evidence for female testosterone therapy. (iStock)

"We're left to kind of decide, 'Well, what now?'" Dombo said. "It's all experimentation. ... We don't have a set guideline for how to be able to do this for women. We have to rely on the art of medicine."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
The latest federal meeting represents a critical step forward, according to Dombo, who believes grassroots advocacy from patients and clinicians is forcing regulatory action.
"We're not going to stop knocking on the door because there are several of us who believe that women deserve to be able to have access to just what they need," she said.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"Sexual health is part of your entire health," Dombo emphasized, expressing optimism that regulatory agencies will eventually adapt to support safer, standardized access.
Khloe Quill is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital. She and the lifestyle team cover a range of story topics including food and drink, travel, and health.

title: Kim Kardashian reveals new health scare with haunting connection to father’s cancer death
summary: Kim Kardashian reveals her esophagitis diagnosis in a new "Kardashians" trailer, raising fears tied to her father's esophageal cancer death.
story: Dr. Brian M. Slomovitz, director of gynecologic oncology at Mount Sinai Medical Center in Miami Beach, Florida, says ovarian cancer was once known as the ‘silent killer,’ meaning it was often undetected until it reached an advanced stage.
Kim Kardashian is opening up about a new health diagnosis that hits close to home.
In a new trailer for "The Kardashians," the reality star, 45, revealed that she has esophagitis, which is inflammation of the esophagus.
The diagnosis held a particular significance given that her father, Robert Kardashian Sr., died of esophageal cancer in 2003 at age 59.
ALCOHOL TIED TO SURPRISING CANCER DEATH PATTERN IN ADULTS UNDER 55, RESEARCHERS FIND
In the episode, the Skims founder is seen lying on a hospital bed as someone off camera asks, "Didn’t your father ... isn’t it what he died of?"
In a new trailer for "The Kardashians," Kim Kardashian revealed she has esophagitis, which is inflammation of the esophagus. (Getty Images)
Kardashian’s manager and mother, Kris Jenner, became emotional at this suggestion, saying, "I can’t. It makes me want to cry."
Experts have noted, however, that the two conditions are not the same.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

Kim Kardashian's diagnosis, esophagitis, is an inflammation of the esophagus, the muscular tube that carries food from the throat to the stomach. It is most commonly caused by acid reflux, certain medications, infections or allergies, according to the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK).
The diagnosis held a particular significance given that her father, Robert Kardashian Sr., died of esophageal cancer in 2003 at age 59. (Getty Images)

Esophageal cancer occurs when malignant cells form in the tissues lining the esophagus, according to the National Cancer Institute. There are two main types: squamous cell carcinoma and adenocarcinoma.

While esophagitis itself does not directly cause cancer, the chronic inflammation can in some cases lead to Barrett's esophagus, a precancerous condition that can increase the higher risk of esophageal adenocarcinoma. This risk is higher among those with ongoing acid reflux (GERD).
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
About 5% to 15% of people with GERD develop Barrett's esophagus, although most people with Barrett's do not develop esophageal cancer, the NIDDK states.
Robert Kardashian and daughter Kim Kardashian stand outside of her private high school, Marymount High School, in Los Angeles, in 1996. (Getty Images)
For those who have been diagnosed with esophagitis, the Mayo Clinic provides the following recommendations to manage symptoms and reduce future cancer risk.

title: Celebrity plastic surgeon reveals when it's too soon for a facelift, and when waiting can backfire
summary: Dr. Terry Dubrow reveals why Kris Jenner's public facelift is driving 38-year-olds to seek facelift surgery they don't yet need.
story: During an episode of Josh Peck’s podcast, "Good Guys," the Beverly Hills plastic surgeon weighs in on growing demand for cosmetic procedures among younger adults and explains why patients with early skin laxity may be better served by waiting.
When it comes to getting a facelift, timing may be everything.
Going under the knife too soon could mean having surgery before it’s necessary — but waiting too long can also backfire, according to celebrity plastic surgeon Dr. Terry Dubrow.
During an episode of Josh Peck’s and Ben Soffer's podcast, "Good Guys," the Beverly Hills-based surgeon said some women are jumping the gun and getting the procedure too soon.
CHEAP SURGERY OVERSEAS MAY COME WITH DEVASTATING COMPLICATIONS, DOCTORS WARN
"For those people in their 30s who want some skin tightening, they need to wait, 'cause there will be the technology that will allow early facelifts without cutting," he said.
Dubrow also mentioned Kris Jenner’s recent facelift, which may have motivated women to seek out the procedure based on her results.
Going under the knife too soon could mean having surgery before it’s necessary — but waiting too long can also backfire, according to a celebrity plastic surgeon. (iStock)
"That made facelifts like, ‘Oh, Kris Jenner did it and made it public. Now it's cool. Everybody get a facelift,’" he said.

"So then you're seeing 38-year-old people in your office wanting a facelift, and you go, ‘OK, hold on a second. You don't even need a facelift. You need to wait, because, you know, a facelift is incisions and scars, and elevating up the skin, numbness and all sorts of potential things that can go wrong."
MEN FACE NEW PRESSURE TO STAY ‘HOT’ AS THEY AGE — AND IT’S NOT JUST ABOUT LIVING LONGER
Dubrow warned that if people have too many facelifts, "when it starts to relax, it can relax in weird ways."
"You've all seen it — people who look pretty good, but there's something about the way their skin lies on their face that looks unnatural, and it ruins the whole look," he warned.
Dr. Terry Dubrow warned that if people have too many facelifts, "when it starts to relax, it can relax in weird ways." (Getty Images)
"If you have early laxity, don't go in for your ‘Kris Jenner facelift.’ Still wait, because that technology is just around the corner."

Conversely, the surgeon has warned that waiting too long — while relying on other nonsurgical fixes — can also backfire. "A lot of women are staying on the ‘nonsurgical treadmill’ for too long," Dubrow told Fox News Digital.
DO RED LIGHT THERAPY AND COLD PLUNGES REALLY WORK? A DOCTOR REVEALS THE TRUTH
"They keep adding filler, lasers and tightening treatments, when the real problem is that the deeper tissues have dropped."

While it is possible to get a great result with a later-in-life facelift, the doctor pointed out that as the skin becomes looser, the tissues descend further, which may require more extensive surgery.

While it is possible to get a great result with a later-in-life facelift, the doctor pointed out that as the skin becomes looser, the tissues descend further, which may require more extensive surgery. (iStock)
"My feeling is that once those treatments stop producing a natural result, continuing to postpone surgery can actually make you look less natural."
That’s not to say that nonsurgical treatments don’t have their place, he noted.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
"Fillers, lasers and tightening treatments can buy you time when they are used intelligently — but fillers cannot lift sagging tissue, and too much filler can make someone look distorted."
"The right time should be based on your face, not the doctor’s menu."

Aggressive energy treatments can also create scarring under the skin and make surgery more difficult later, Dubrow cautioned — "so, ask whether a treatment is truly delaying a facelift or just delaying the decision."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
There is no "magic age" in terms of best results with a facelift, according to Dubrow.
"For some women, it is their late 40s. For others, it is their 50s or 60s," he said. "It comes down to genetics, skin quality and what is happening along the jawline and neck."
Advice for facelift timing can vary depending on what type of expert you see, and every specialist tends to see the problem through the treatments they perform, the doctor noted.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"A dermatologist may explain what can still be accomplished without surgery, and a board-certified plastic surgeon can tell you when those options have reached their limit … and when it is time to actually reposition the anatomy," he said.
Ultimately, he suggests getting opinions from both sides.

"The right time should be based on your face, not the doctor’s menu," Dubrow said. "Choose what makes sense for your anatomy, your goals and your tolerance for surgery."
"The best facelift is the one nobody knows you had, but the best advice often comes from hearing more than one point of view."

title: Trump FDA pick repeatedly sidesteps Sanders' universal healthcare demands in heated clash
summary: Bernie Sanders pressed Trump FDA nominee Dr. Heidi Overton on whether healthcare is a human right, growing frustrated as she declined to give a yes-or-no answer.
story: Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., pressed Dr. Heidi Overton on healthcare access and prescription drug costs during her confirmation hearing to succeed Marty Makary as FDA commissioner.

Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., repeatedly pressed President Donald Trump's pick to lead the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to endorse universal healthcare as a "human right" Thursday, growing frustrated as the nominee declined to give him the yes-or-no answer he sought.

Dr. Heidi Overton, a physician who completed her residency at Johns Hopkins in Baltimore before joining the America First Policy Institute, faced off with the Vermont independent as she seeks to replace Dr. Marty Makary, who resigned earlier this year amid disagreement with the Trump administration over flavored vapes.

"Do you happen to believe that healthcare is a human right that should be available to every man, woman and child in our country?" Sanders pressed, arguing that the U.S. is the only major country not to guarantee healthcare and that thousands die because of a lack of access and affordability.
TRUMP TO NOMINATE DR HEIDI OVERTON AS NEXT FDA COMMISSIONER
Overton replied that access to healthcare is very important and said she looks forward to carrying out policies and responsibilities "vested from Congress" to the FDA.
Sanders said Overton was not answering his question and tried again.
"I live 50 miles away from the Canadian border," said Sanders, who hails from Burlington. "Somehow everybody in that country can go to a doctor."
Overton said she understands the importance of access to care and believes in getting patients the "best care possible."
Sanders then moved on, saying he was running out of time.
He then pressed Overton on whether President Donald Trump was truthful when he said the U.S. had gone from paying the world's highest prescription drug prices to the lowest.
IF TRUMP WANTS TO LOWER DRUG PRICES, HIS OBVIOUS FREE-RIDING TARGETS ARE OUTSIDE THE US
Dr. Heidi Overton speaks during a healthcare affordability event in the South Court Auditorium of The White House in Washington, D.C., on May 18, 2026. (Kent NISHIMURA / AFP via Getty Images)
The nominee replied that 89% of branded drugs are covered by agreements to lower prices for U.S. consumers.
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

"The most-favored nation-policies have dropped prices and right now CPI says that for the first time in 60 years prescription drug prices have gone down by 3%," Overton said, citing a framework championed by Trump. Sanders disputed what caused the decline.

Senator Bernie Sanders, an Independent from Vermont and ranking member of the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, arrives for a confirmation hearing in Washington, DC, US, on Wednesday, July 16, 2025. (Valerie Plesch/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"Yeah, which may have something to do with the legislation that we passed several years ago," he said. The broader debate over Medicare for all and other government-run healthcare proposals is also playing out ahead of November’s midterm elections.

title: EXCLUSIVE: DHS Secretary Mullin slams sanctuary politicians as attacks on ICE officers skyrocket
summary: Assaults against ICE officers surged 1,649% since Trump took office, and DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin blames sanctuary politicians and anti-ICE riots.
story: Border 'czar' Tom Homan discusses the ICE shooting in Austin, Texas, on 'The Will Cain Show.'

FIRST ON FOX: Assaults against U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers have steadily increased in recent months by 1,649% with many incidents fueled by opposition to the Trump administration's crackdown on illegal immigration.

There were 647 assaults against ICE personnel from Jan. 20, 2025, through Sept. 20, 2026, compared to just 37 under the Biden administration from Jan. 20, 2021, to Sept. 20, 2022, according to the Department of Homeland Security.

"The brave men and women of ICE, who are simply enforcing the laws mandated by Congress and protecting the American people, are under attack every single day. Since President Trump unleashed ICE to do their jobs, assaults against them have risen by more than 1,600% in the first year and a half of the administration," said DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin.
HEROIC ICE OFFICERS, STAFF MEMBER OPEN UP ON GROWING DANGERS: ‘AM I GOING TO DIE?'

Attacks against U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers have increased 1,649%, the Department of Homeland Security said. ICE officers have faced assaults, threats and increased political rhetoric, the agency said. One Houston ICE officer suffered a severe laceration, requiring 13 stitches, and burns to the face, in an assault by an illegal immigrant, according to DHS. (Department of Homeland Security)
Mullin blamed the backlash against ICE on "vicious lies" being spread by "sanctuary politicians and their foot soldiers who are involved in anti-ICE riots and other acts of violence."

"DHS is calling on these sanctuary politicians to stop attacking federal law enforcement, stop putting the needs of illegal aliens ahead of the safety of American citizens, and to start working with us to make America safe again," he added.
DEMOCRAT COMPARES ICE TO 'DOMESTIC TERRORISTS' AS 111 HOUSE DEMS DEMAND TEXAS DETENTION CENTER CLOSE
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers have been assaulted and injured during law enforcement operations, officials said. (Department of Homeland Security)

DHS cited examples of mainly Democratic elected officials accusing ICE of terrorizing communities and threatening public safety despite the agency arresting many individuals with criminal records that include convictions for murder, child sex crimes, terrorism and drug trafficking, among others.

Some congressional lawmakers have called for the abolition of the agency, while others have compared ICE to "the SS" and "the Gestapo," the two primary and most feared instruments of terror, surveillance and control in Nazi Germany. Rep. Jasmine Crockett, D-Texas, likened the agency to "slave patrols" that were "disappearing people based on their skin color."

In addition, some anti-ICE protesters have brandished weapons at officers, made threats, thrown objects and impeded law enforcement operations, DHS said. In October 2025, Eduardo Aguilar, an illegal immigrant from Mexico living in Dallas, Texas, was arrested after allegedly posting a video on TikTok in Spanish soliciting the murder of ICE personnel.
DEM RHODE ISLAND LAWMAKER THREATENS ICE: 'YOUR DAY OF RECKONING WILL COME M----- F------'
Authorities have confiscated weapons and ammunition used against U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers. (Department of Homeland Security; iStock)

In July 2025, a group of anti-ICE protesters opened fire on ICE officers at the Prairieland Detention Center in Alvarado, Texas, wounding a law enforcement officer. Eight suspects tied to that case were sentenced in June to prison terms ranging from 30 to 100 years.

In June 2025, Gabriel Hurtado-Cariaco, a member of the Tren de Aragua gang in Bellevue, Nebraska, was accused of throwing an ICE agent to the ground, slamming her head into the pavement, ripping off her body armor and making repeated physical violent contact during an attempted arrest, authorities said.
The agent sustained serious injuries to her head and arm and was taken to the University of Nebraska Medical Center for treatment. Hurtado-Cariaco was charged with attempted murder.
PORTLAND MAN SENTENCED TO 30 MONTHS IN PRISON FOR THROWING ROCK AT ICE OFFICER DURING PROTEST
The Prairieland Detention Facility in Alvarado, Texasm where a police officer was shot in the neck and several ICE officers were shot at July 4, 2025. (KDFW)
Others have allegedly attacked ICE officers with rocks, Molotov cocktails and various other objects, officials said.
The backlash against ICE has intensified amid the Trump administration's targeting of illegal immigrants with criminal records and those with final removal orders.
DHS BOSS REVEALS OVAL OFFICE PLAN TO 'WITHHOLD FUNDING' FROM SANCTUARY CITIES AFTER AGGRESSIVE NEW YORK BUST

Many Democratic-run jurisdictions have beefed up their sanctuary policies to prevent cooperation between local law enforcement and federal immigration authorities.

title: Dems shamed as DHS brings ICE shooting receipts after politician called ICE officers ‘liars with masks’
summary: The Department of Homeland Security accused Democrats and media of spreading lies about the ICE shooting in Austin as protests erupted citywide.
story: Bodycam footage released by the Austin Police Department shows the aftermath of the shooting of Wilber Rafael Garces Perez (Credit: Austin Police Department).

The Department of Homeland Security called out dozens of Democrats and members of the media for "spreading lies" about a recent ICE officer-involved shooting in Austin, while a former agency director suggested the political response may be by design.

Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, a 28-year-old Venezuelan national whom DHS says is an illegal immigrant in the U.S., was shot by an ICE agent during a chase Sunday. Perez was arrested and taken to a nearby hospital, where he was treated and listed in stable condition. The shooting has prompted protests in Austin and criticism from Democrats.

On Tuesday, more than 100 Democratic members of Congress signed a letter demanding Perez’s release and saying he "is not receiving the care he needs in detention" and "still has the bullet lodged in his body."

In a separate statement, Rep. Joaquin Castro, D-Texas, said "despite losing movement on his left side and having a bullet lodged next to his spine, ICE has forced Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez out of the hospital and back to the South Texas ICE Processing Center." Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, called ICE "liars with masks" and demanded the agency leave Austin.
DEM REACTIONS WITHIN MOMENTS OF AUSTIN ICE SHOOTING SPARK VIRAL OUTRAGE LOCALLY, ONLINE: 'DISQUALIFYING'

Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, speaks during a news conference at the Law Office of Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch in Austin on Monday, Sept. 21, 2026, about the previous day’s shooting of Wilber Rafael Garces Perez by an ICE agent. (Austin American-Statesman/Hearst Newspapers/Contributor via Getty Images)

In response, DHS posted on X that "sanctuary politicians and the media wasted no time in spreading lies" and that "no amount of smears and false narratives will slow down ICE from doing its job to arrest illegal aliens from our communities."

DHS called the claim that ICE refused to remove the bullet from Perez’s body "false." The agency said ICE "does not and would not advise, nor be the authority on, a medical procedure for an illegal alien at a hospital." Addressing reports that Perez was denied pain medication and made to sleep on the floor, DHS said Perez is "receiving medical care around the clock, including pain medication," and that after being released from the hospital, he slept on a bed a few hours after arriving at ICE’s detention facility.

The agency also disputed statements from Perez’s lawyer that Perez entered the country legally and has a work permit. DHS said he "entered the country illegally under the Biden Administration" and "had no valid work permit, had no protective status, and had a final order of removal from a Department of Justice (DOJ) Immigration Judge."
FEDERAL JUDGE TEMPORARILY BLOCKS DEPORTATION OF ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT SHOT BY ICE OFFICER IN AUSTIN, ATTORNEY SAYS
Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, 28, an illegal immigrant from Venezuela, was shot by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers in Austin, Texas, over the weekend. (Wilber Garces/Facebook)
DHS said ICE "will not be slowing down nor leaving Austin."
"DHS is tasked with enforcing the laws passed by Congress. We do not pick and choose which laws to enforce or where to enforce them. We will continue to enforce our nation’s laws," the agency said.
Former acting ICE Director Jonathan Fahey, who served toward the end of President Donald Trump’s first term, suggested some of the political pushback was by design.

"The irony of it all is, with these ICE incidents, it's not just coincidental that the Democrats are against ICE performing their function of enforcing immigration laws… they don't want them actually doing their jobs," Fahey said in an interview with Fox News Digital.
"They try to build these situations up to try to get negative attention toward ICE and more political pressure on them and advance their political agenda."

Fahey suggested the Democratic Party’s "whole goal" is an open Mexican border and mass amnesty. He argued that Democrats’ response to the Austin incident shows they do not want what he considers responsible enforcement, but no enforcement.

"They seem to have doubled down on [the 'mass amnesty' agenda] after the 2024 election, which in some respects is surprising," he said. "My opinion is their motive is… for the people here open the border because they think that will help them electorally currently and in the future – and all the other stuff is just noise to help achieve that."
BRANDON GILL UNLOADS ON DEMOCRATS OVER ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT CHARGED WITH RAPING TEEN: 'COLLATERAL DAMAGE'
People protest against Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers on Sept. 20, 2026, in Austin, Texas. An ICE officer shot and wounded a person earlier in North Austin. (Brandon Bell/Getty Images)

Asked about Casar’s demands that DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin "preserve every piece of evidence," suspend the agent in question and brief Congress, Fahey said it would be irresponsible for DHS to brief Congress before the investigation is complete.
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

"That's mostly going to be a distraction," he said. "Congress wants to exercise oversight over this particular instance. I think the more appropriate thing would be after DHS has concluded their investigation [for] all of that [to be] done. I don't think the secretary would have any issue preserving evidence. I think they'll be doing that anyway."

"I don't think that's a concern. But turning stuff over for hearing this early seems premature at the least," he said.
Peter Pinedo is a politics writer for Fox News Digital.

title: 4 GOP senators rebel against Trump on Iran war, vote with Dems to rein in authority
summary: President Donald Trump dismissed midterm fears as Republicans defeated a Democratic war powers resolution despite surging gas and diesel prices.
story: Rep. Claudia Tenney, R-N.Y., discusses President Donald Trump’s prediction that the Iran war will end after the 2026 midterm elections on ‘Fox Report.’
Despite voter fury and rising fuel prices, most Republican senators stayed the course with President Donald Trump and his war on Iran in a vote Thursday.

Though vulnerable Republicans on the campaign trail broke with Trump earlier this week, calling for an "immediate end" to the war, lawmakers on the Hill stuck with him and defeated another attempt by Democrats to rein in his war authorities as the conflict nears the eight-month mark.

Still, there was a group of rebellious Republicans who had consistently voted with Democrats, including Sens. Susan Collins, R-Maine, Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, Rand Paul, R-Ky. New blood was added this time with Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C.
REPUBLICANS BREAK WITH TRUMP TO REBUKE IRAN WAR — BUT IT WON'T CHANGE POLICY
President Donald Trump during the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Sept. 22, 2026. (Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Tillis, who is retiring at the end of the year, argued his decision to vote for the latest war powers resolution came after the administration again blew past a 60-day deadline to involve Congress.

"We know the resolution's not gonna pass, but it is important to start saying, ‘We deserve an update. You better start treating — Congress can be an assistance with this war effort, if you inform us,’" Tillis said.

To Tillis’ point, the resolution that failed in the Senate, which passed in the House with seven Republican defectors, would have headed to the president’s desk, where it likely would have been vetoed. And without a veto-proof majority, the effort wouldn't have teeth legally. However, it will hurt on the airwaves in the ads to come.
GOP CRACKS WIDEN OVER IRAN WAR AS VULNERABLE CANDIDATES BREAK WITH TRUMP, DEMAND ITS END

Thursday’s vote comes as Republicans are getting an earful about the war, particularly over skyrocketing gas and diesel prices, on the campaign trail. Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., acknowledged that fuel prices are a growing issue for Americans.
"Well, I think people are, there's voter fatigue with high gas prices and high diesel prices in my part of the world," Thune said.

"So, that's a frustration, it's an economic frustration, and that's why, again, I hope the administration is laser-focused on trying to get the [Strait of Hormuz] open, get the shipping lights opened up, and help out with that global energy supply, because that ultimately will get prices down," he continued.

Three vulnerable Republicans running for toss-up seats this week, Rep. Ashley Hinson, R-Iowa, former Rep. Mike Rogers in Michigan, and Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio, all requested that the fighting come to an "immediate end" as the war grows in unpopularity with their voters.
TRUMP DEFENDS US INTERVENTIONS ABROAD AHEAD OF 'BIG DECISION' ON IRAN: 'SETTLING YEARS OF UNFINISHED BUSINESS'
Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., plans to force a vote on his war powers resolution to rein in President Donald Trump's military action in Iran. (Graeme Sloan/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., who has acted as the self-anointed traffic cop for the deluge of Democratic war powers resolutions over the last several months, diagnosed the defections as a by-product of reports that U.S. bombs had fallen on an Iranian school and that diesel costs are "going up and up and up."

"They are listening to their constituents. They should [have] listened to them before now, because their constituents were saying, ‘Don't get into this thing,’" Kaine said. "But they're finally listening to them. And nothing makes you listen as much as an election staring you in the face."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
But Trump isn’t swayed by the effects that the conflict could have on the midterm elections as the GOP fights to keep power in Congress.

"The Republican Party is running, and I'll be helping them, but I am not running," Trump told reporters this week. "I gave absolutely no credence and will not give credence to the election when it comes to Iran. It doesn't even enter my mind. The only thing that does is that Iran will never have a nuclear weapon."
Alex Miller is a writer for Fox News Digital covering the U.S. Senate.

title: James Copenhaver, man shot at Trump Butler rally, dies of complications from injuries: report
summary: James Copenhaver, who was wounded in the 2024 assassination attempt on President Donald Trump in Butler, Pennsylvania, has died, according to several reports.
story: Associated Press chief DC photographer Evan Vucci joins 'The Sunday Briefing' to discuss capturing the iconic Butler image, how he spotted a major scoop in real time and what it’s like documenting President Donald Trump’s return to office.
James Copenhaver, of Coraopolis, Pennsylvania, who was wounded in a failed assassination attempt on President Donald Trump in 2024, has died, according to several reports.

Copenhaver, in his mid-70s, was one of several people who attempted assassin Thomas Matthew Crooks shot at the Butler Farm Show complex outside Butler, Pennsylvania, after Crooks scaled the roof of a nearby glass manufacturing building and took aim at the then-presidential candidate.
A person who answered a phone number connected to Copenhaver's family directed Fox News Digital to a Pittsburgh-area law firm for confirmation and further comment.
GOP LAWMAKERS BLINDSIDED BY NEW REVELATIONS ABOUT TRUMP BUTLER SHOOTER: ‘AWFULLY STRANGE’
James Copenhaver, one of the victims in the Trump assassination attempt in Butler, Pa. (Handout)
The House Republican Conference posted an obituary for Copenhaver on social media, saying he had died Thursday and that lawmakers were "deeply saddened."

"Jim endured unimaginable hardship with strength and perseverance. We join his family and loved ones in mourning his loss and praying for them during this difficult time. May he rest in peace," the caucus said in a statement.

Ken Silva, a journalist who wrote a book about the assassination attempt, wrote on his website that a person close to Copenhaver's family also confirmed Copenhaver had died and had been dealing with permanent injuries, including bullet fragments still lodged in his body.
David Dutch was also wounded in the shooting but survived. Butler County firefighter Corey Comperatore was shot and killed in the bleachers behind Trump’s dais that day.
Speaking to Pittsburgh's KDKA in 2025, Copenhaver said he stood to look at the jumbotron behind him as Trump spoke.
https://www.foxnews.com/us/trump-supporter-pennsylvania-rally-recounts-harrowing-attempted-assassination-moments?utm_source=chatgpt.com
TRUMP SUPPORTER AT PENNSYLVANIA RALLY RECOUNTS HARROWING ATTEMPTED ASSASSINATION MOMENTS
"Next thing I know, my sleeve has been yanked," he said. "I could see a portion of it going by pretty fast, and I heard 'pew.' I heard it, and I didn't realize at the time that I had gotten shot."
He said he was then shot a second time but that the bullets both "went into soft material."
"It was like a jolt. It didn't knock me over, but I didn't want to stand anymore," he told the station.
A lawsuit Copenhaver filed against the United States earlier this year alleged he was also required to undergo multiple surgeries.
Mayor Jondavid Longo of nearby Slippery Rock, Pennsylvania — who spoke at the Butler rally — mourned Copenhaver’s reported death Thursday.
Secret Service missed ‘multiple opportunities’ to prevent Trump assassination attempt: watchdog
SECRET SERVICE MISSED ‘MULTIPLE OPPORTUNITIES’ TO PREVENT TRUMP ASSASSINATION ATTEMPT: WATCHDOG
Law enforcement officers gather at the campaign rally site for in Butler, Pa., after the attempted assassination of former President Donald Trump, July 13, 2024. (AP Photo/Evan Vucci)

"[Copenhaver] survived that day, but he never fully recovered from the wounds. For two years he lived with surgeries, remaining fragments, and pain that never left him. Those of us who were there that day have never forgotten Corey Comperatore, David Dutch, or Jim," Longo said in a statement on X.
"Butler County still carries that afternoon. May he rest in peace. Prayers for Marianne and the Copenhaver family."

The attack triggered intense scrutiny of the Secret Service after investigations uncovered breakdowns in planning, communication and security around the rally site. Then-Secret Service Director Kimberly Cheatle resigned less than two weeks later, taking responsibility for the security lapse. A subsequent bipartisan House task force concluded the Butler attack was preventable and identified failures in planning, execution and leadership.
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

One of the Republican lawmakers on that task force, Rep. Carlos Gimenez of Florida, climbed onto the roof Crooks used to take aim at Trump and later told Fox News Digital he was incredulous at how easy it was to scale after Cheatle had cited the roof’s slope in explaining why it was not secured.
CLICK HERE TO GET THE FOX NEWS APP
President Trump raises his fist after the assassination attempt on his life in Butler, Pennsylvania, in July 2024. (Rebecca Droke/AFP via Getty Images)
Six Secret Service agents were later suspended without pay in connection with the failures.
Trump returned to Butler in October 2024, less than three months after the assassination attempt, to hold another rally at the same site and honor Comperatore.

Trump’s raised fist and mouthing of the word "fight" became a lasting image of the assassination attempt that he used throughout his successful campaign to become the first president since Grover Cleveland to serve two nonconsecutive terms.
This is a developing story. Check back for updates.
Born and raised in Allentown, Pennsylvania, worked in both the New York and Washington bureaus for Fox News since 2013.

title: Alaska has a voting system like no other state; Republicans worry it could cost them in November
summary: Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan faces Mary Peltola in Alaska's ranked choice voting Senate race, complicated by a "Decoy Dan" candidate on the ballot.
story: GOP strategist Mary Marslender warns in a Fox News Digital interview that Alaska’s unique election system is ‘hurting’ Republicans in crucial Senate race.

Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan is in the middle of a competitive race as he seeks re-election this year in red-leaning Alaska in a midterm showdown that's one of roughly a dozen that will determine if the GOP keeps control of the Senate.

Working against Sullivan as he runs for a third six-year term in the Senate is not only a rough political climate facing Republicans but also Alaska's unique electoral system, which includes four candidates from an open primary advancing to the general election and ranked-choice voting.

Alaska is the only state in the nation to have a "top four" primary system in which candidates advance regardless of party affiliation. And it's one of only two states, along with Maine, to use ranked choice voting for statewide and federal races.
Defenders of the system say it gives independent voters more choices, weakens party control and encourages candidates to appeal beyond their base.
SEEING DOUBLE: THE SECOND DAN SULLIVAN ADVANCES IN ALASKA'S CRUCIAL SENATE SHOWDOWN
Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska, speaks during a hearing with the Senate Armed Services Committee in the Dirksen Senate Office Building April 30, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)
Alaska GOP Chair Carmela Warfield has repeatedly referred to the state's electoral system as a "MESS" in social media posts.
"It's hurting the Republican Party," veteran GOP strategist Mary Marslender told Fox News Digital.
Sullivan is battling former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola. The two candidates combined received over 90% of the primary vote.
But Daniel J. Sullivan, a retired schoolteacher and registered Republican whom Marslender and supporters of the senator call "Decoy Dan" is also on the general election ballot.

A conservative nonprofit group, Americans for Public Trust, claimed that the other Sullivan, who is not related to the senator, was working with Democrats to confuse voters. The Peltola campaign and Daniel J. Sullivan both denied the allegation.
The Alaska Division of Elections disqualified him from the ballot, but the decision was overturned first by an Alaska Superior Court judge and later by the state Supreme Court.
SIX FORCES THAT COULD HELP REPUBLICANS DEFY HISTORY IN THE MIDTERM ELECTIONS
Dan J. Sullivan, who has filed to run for U.S. Senate in Alaska, poses for a photo in Petersburg, Alaska, June 26, 2026. (Katie Holmlund/Associated Press)
There is also a third Republican on the Senate ballot: Gerald Heikes. He advanced to the general election when the fourth-place primary finisher, Democrat David Leslie, withdrew from the race.
Marslender claimed that the current system has "become an easy way for the Democrats to game the system."

Pointing to Daniel J. Sullivan's inclusion on the general election ballot, she said, "That never would have been allowed in the previous old system. … But because there's an open primary, he was allowed to be on the ballot.
"Republican primary voters under the old system wouldn't have voted for him, and he wouldn't have been in there."
With ranked-choice voting, voters rank candidates by preference, and if nobody receives a majority of first-choice votes, additional counting rounds occur until someone reaches a majority.
Marslender said there's a perception that Republicans would unite around the incumbent senator in the general election.
DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB
Former Rep. Mary Peltola, D-Alaska, is running for the U.S. Senate in the 2026 midterm elections. (Nathan Posner/Anadolu)
But, she said, in Alaska, which is the nation's largest and most remote state, "It's really hard to get a statewide message out" due to "the geographical challenges."
Alaskans for Better Elections, which supports the system, has been holding events to help voters better understand how it works.
"Alaska’s election system celebrates our independence, giving us the freedom to vote for the person who is best for the job," the group highlights on its website.

The Senate race wasn't the only contest impacted by the current system. There were also eleventh-hour withdrawals that rocked the races for governor and the U.S. House, which also cast a shadow on the state's unique voting process.
Alaska voters get to weigh in when they cast general election ballots to either keep or scrap the current system.

Matt Schultz, a Democrat who suspended his congressional bid before the primary, supports keeping the system. But he told the AP, "We need to make things much more transparent and predictable and understandable by the general public so that we can truly have trust in our democracy again."
Republican Lesil McGuire and Democrat Tom Begich, former state lawmakers who were both eliminated in the primary for governor, defended the system.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"Let’s be clear: We would have faced challenges and might not have advanced in a traditional closed or semi-closed primary. Our election system was not designed to guarantee anyone a win. It was designed to solve a problem: elections in which a narrow, more partisan slice of voters decided the November ballot, resulting in hyperpartisanship that limited progress," they wrote in an opinion piece in The Anchorage Daily News.
"We don’t support our current system because it was good for us as candidates; we support it because it’s good for us as Alaskans."
Paul Steinhauser covers the national campaign trail from coast to coast for Fox News

title: Canadian PM Carney says he was prepared for Trump ordering invasion
summary: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney says he weighed the possibility of a U.S. invasion after Trump began calling Canada the 51st state amid tariffs.
story: President Donald Trump calls Canada a 'terrible trade partner' and warns Europe could face heavy tariffs, as Mark Carney’s anti-Trump strategy takes focus.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney says he prepared for the "extreme tail risk" that the U.S. would invade Canada amid recent trade tensions.
Carney made the statement in an interview with The New York Times published Wednesday, saying he weighed the possibility after President Donald Trump began referring to Canada as the 51st state.

"I think you have a responsibility in these roles to look at extreme tail risk. That’s just risk management. That’s not a base case," Carney told the Times, arguing that "it would be irresponsible not to."
CANADIAN PM TELLS TRUMP TO 'STOP TRYING TO BE TOUGH' IN TRADE FIGHT
Mark Carney, Canada's prime minister, speaks during a news conference in Ottawa, Ontario, Canada, March 27, 2025.  (David Kawai/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Trade tensions between the U.S. and Canada have continued to escalate over the past year, with Trump levying increased tariffs and Canada responding in kind.
Carney admitted in a video statement earlier this month that Canada had come to overly rely on its economic relationship with the U.S. in recent decades.
FORMER BIDEN AMBASSADOR BLAMES TRUMP FOR CANADA PLAYING 'FOOTSIE' WITH CHINA
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney is greeted by President Donald Trump as he arrives at the West Wing of the White House May 6, 2025, in Washington. (AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein)

"The past 40 years has been a period of deeper economic integration with the United States. Truth is, it was easy business, but it meant we relied too much on one economic partner. It’s clear that time is over," Carney said.
"This is why our plan, since I came into office, has been development and diversification, not denial, waiting to go back to some good old days and not continued dependence."
FEARS OF A CANADIAN TRADE WAR ARE OVERBLOWN; SO FAR, IT’S MORE OF A SKIRMISH

Trump last week dismissed reports that Canada may be joining the European Union as an associate member, saying the U.S. could impose heavy tariffs on Europe if he believed such a "laughable" move was made with "bad intention."
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney delivers a speech at the World Economic Forum Annual Meeting held in Davos, Switzerland, Jan. 20, 2026. (Harun Ozalp/Anadolu via Getty Images)
"I think it's laughable," Trump responded. "If they do that, if I think it's at all a hostile act, I will put very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe on many things.

"If Europe does that with a bad intention — if it's a good intention, that's fine — if it's a bad intention, we'll put very heavy tariffs on Europe."
Anders Hagstrom is a reporter with Fox News Digital covering national politics and major breaking news events.

title: Soros-linked prosecutor faces primary challenge as fellow Democrat targets his record
summary: Fairfax County Commonwealth's Attorney Stephen Descano faces a Democratic primary challenge from a former federal prosecutor citing botched cases.
story: Former acting I.C.E. director Jonathan Fahey criticizes Fairfax Commonwealth’s Attorney Steve Descano for allegedly offering lenient treatment to illegal immigrant defendants on 'America Reports.'
Fairfax County Commonwealth’s Attorney Stephen Descano is facing a forceful rebuke from a former federal prosecutor who extensively criticized his record after announcing her bid to unseat him.

Descano, a Democrat, has faced criticism over what opponents describe as lenient prosecutorial decisions, particularly in serious cases involving illegal immigrant suspects. Former federal prosecutor Brittany Dunn-Pirio said that if there weren’t systemic problems in his office, she would want to work there.

"If this office were doing its job, I wouldn’t be running against it. I’d be applying to work for it. But it isn’t," Dunn-Pirio said on her new campaign website after Washington, D.C.-area media reported her bid late Wednesday.
VIRGINIA DEMS SPLIT ON DOJ PROBE OF SOROS-BACKED DA ACCUSED OF GIVING 'SWEETHEART DEALS' TO ILLEGAL ALIENS

"I’m a Democrat. This race isn’t about whether reform was right. It’s about whether the office can tell the difference between a first-time nonviolent offender who deserves a second chance and a violent or sexual offender who doesn’t," Dunn-Pirio said on her website.
"It’s about whether deadlines are met, evidence is given to the defendant and victims are spoken to."
VIRGINIA DEM DEFENDS SOROS-BACKED PROSECUTOR FROM DOJ PROBE AFTER ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT CHARGING ALLEGATIONS
Fairfax County Commonwealth's Attorney Steve Descano, left, and Fairfax County Sheriff Stacey Ann Kincaid, right, testify before Congress. (Tom Williams/Getty Images)
Fox News Digital reached out to Descano and Dunn-Pirio for further comment.

Descano campaign spokesman Nathan Kiker defended the incumbent's record, telling Fox News Digital that "Steve Descano has spent his tenure proving that you can reform the justice system and keep our community safe at the same time."

"Today, Fairfax County is recognized as the safest large county in the nation because Steve focused on accountability and the root causes of crime rather than failed policies of the past. We are proud to put that record before the voters," Kiker said.
Dunn-Pirio also pointed to "botched sexual assault cases" and prosecutors declining to meet with victims, along with her contention that the justice system too often favors the "well-connected."

One case that has drawn the scrutiny of Descano’s office involves Abdul Jalloh, an illegal immigrant from Sierra Leone charged with murdering Stephanie Minter. Minter was stabbed and killed at a Hybla Valley bus stop in February after Jalloh had cycled through the criminal justice system following numerous previous arrests.
Descano has pushed back on claims that his office simply allowed Jalloh to walk free, telling Congress his prosecutors obtained convictions against him "wherever possible."
SOROS-BACKED DA'S LAX ILLEGAL IMMIGRATION POLICIES LED TO 'PREVENTABLE' BUS STOP STABBING MURDER: COMPLAINT

Nine of the illegal immigrants charged with serious crimes in Fairfax County in 2026, left to right from top: Juan Arevalo Mendez, Moises Domingo Rico Rosales, Cristian Wilfredo Alvarenga Aguilar, Walvin Victor Hugo Garcia, Roni Mendez-Escobar, Israel Christopher Flores-Ortiz, Misael Lopez Gomez, Maldin Anibal Guzman-Videz, Luis Alonzo Sort-Portillo. (DHS)

Dunn-Pirio previously served as a prosecutor in Frederick County, Virginia, and as a federal prosecutor in the district covering Lexington, Kentucky. She said she resigned from the DOJ in 2025 after working on COVID-related fraud and similar cases.
"I couldn’t stomach propping up a system that gave pardons to the well-connected while prosecuting average Americans for the same conduct," she said, according to a release obtained by FairfaxNow.
She also said Descano’s office has spent too much time "failing the people I care about."
A carousel on her new campaign website highlights cases that have drawn public scrutiny of Descano, including:
REPEAT OFFENDER WITH DOZENS OF PRIOR CHARGES ARRESTED FOR BURGLARIZING CHURCH IN SOROS-BACKED DA'S COUNTY

"We need a Commonwealth’s Attorney who can make this office work," Dunn-Pirio said. "Every person in Fairfax should feel safe, and every person in Fairfax should be able to trust the office that’s supposed to protect them."
Descano’s campaign did not immediately respond to an additional request for comment on Dunn-Pirio’s criticism.

Dunn-Pirio, most recently an associate at the civil litigation firm Harman, Claytor, Corrigan & Wellman, served as an assistant U.S. attorney in Kentucky for two years before resigning in November 2025. At the Justice Department, she specialized in COVID relief fraud and public corruption cases, according to her LinkedIn profile.

"Most recently I was a federal prosecutor, and I resigned from the Justice Department because I couldn’t stomach propping up a system that gave pardons to the well-connected while prosecuting average Americans for the same conduct," Dunn-Pirio said.

Before becoming a federal prosecutor in 2023, Dunn-Pirio served as an assistant commonwealth’s attorney in Frederick County, an assistant attorney general in the state criminal appeals courts and a law clerk to Judge Randy Bellows in Fairfax County Circuit Court.
Dunn-Pirio emphasized that she is a "cradle Democrat," distinguishing her candidacy from a challenge to Descano from the political right.

She said she volunteered for former Vice President Al Gore at age 9, helped lead the College Democrats at the University of Notre Dame, remains active in local Democratic groups and previously managed a campaign for Virginia Del. Marcus Simon, D-Falls Church.

Republicans hold only one seat on the Fairfax County Board of Supervisors, while Democrats hold the remaining seats. Dunn-Pirio’s challenge to Descano will be decided first in the Democratic nomination contest ahead of the 2027 election.
