title: Can tech really get you off your phone and into real life?
summary: NewTree Social founder Maddy O'Connor built a community events app to help people discover local gatherings, wellness events and run clubs nearby.
story: Kendall Schrohe, co-founder of AttentionSphere.org, discusses how young Americans are participating in a one-month digital detox challenge, swapping smartphones for flip phones.
How many times have you picked up your phone to check one thing and found yourself still scrolling 30 minutes later? I know I've done it.

Our phones make it incredibly easy to stay connected. Yet something interesting seems to be happening at the same time. Many people are looking for more reasons to put those phones down and spend time with other people in the real world.
Run clubs are growing. Local gatherings are drawing attention. Phone-free events are popping up. People seem hungry for experiences that feel a little less like another feed.

That raises an interesting question: Could the same technology that keeps pulling us online also help get us back into real life? That idea is behind NewTree Social, an early-stage community events app from 29-year-old founder Maddy O'Connor. She wants people to use their phones to discover something happening nearby, make a plan and then go experience it. And the timing may be right.
RESTAURANTS BAN DINERS' PHONES DURING MEALS AS NO-SCROLL TREND GROWS: PUT IT AWAY OR ELSE
More people are looking for ways to put their phones down, step away from the screen and spend more time connecting in the real world. (iStock)
NEW! 🩺 Free CyberGuy LIVE class: Get Better Healthcare With AI Saturday, September 26 at 11 a.m. ET / 8 a.m. PT

Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will show you five practical ways AI can help you organize your health history, remember important appointment details, understand complicated medical information, research prescriptions and prepare smarter questions for your doctor. No technical experience is needed.
Save your free spot at CyberGuyLive.com.
More people are looking beyond the screen

There is some real data behind this shift. Eventbrite's 2026 Social Study surveyed people ages 18 to 35 in the U.S. and U.K. It found that 79% planned to attend more events in 2026. Among Gen Z respondents, 46% said they were limiting screen time and 74% said in-person experiences were more important than digital ones.
Now, keep in mind that this research comes from Eventbrite, a company whose business revolves around live events. Still, those numbers line up with something we are seeing play out in the real world.

Eventbrite says phone-free experiences listed on its platform grew 567% globally between 2024 and 2025. Attendance at those events rose 121%. The company based those numbers on events that used "phone-free" terminology in their title or description.

For people who have spent years with a smartphone within arm's reach, intentionally putting it away feels significant. It also creates an unusual opening for technology. Instead of asking how an app can keep you scrolling longer, what if the goal becomes helping you find something worth closing the app for?
One young founder saw an opportunity

That is where O'Connor comes in. She told CyberGuy that the idea for NewTree grew partly from her own experience living in Washington, D.C., without an established group of friends. Her experience changed depending on where she lived and whether she could find places where meeting new people felt natural.
At the same time, she was watching interest grow around run clubs, wellness events, social clubs and other in-person experiences. So she started building around that behavior.
NewTree is designed to help people discover local activities and meet others through something they already want to do. I think that part is important.

Walking into a room of strangers solely because you are supposed to meet people can feel awkward. Walking into a fitness class, community event or gathering you already find interesting gives you a reason to be there before you ever introduce yourself. For someone who recently moved or simply wants to expand a social circle, that could make taking the first step a little easier.
NewTree wants your scrolling to lead somewhere
Open NewTree and the basic experience should feel familiar. There is a feed. You browse events nearby. You can RSVP and get reminders about something you want to attend.

But the idea behind that feed is a little different. O'Connor comes from a graphic design background and told CyberGuy that she deliberately wanted NewTree to feel more like a social platform than a traditional events directory.
The app currently focuses on community, fitness and wellness events around Tampa, St. Pete and Clearwater. Apple describes it as an app for discovering local events, RSVPing and meeting new people.

Hosts can add photos and videos to event listings. Users can browse what is happening around them and RSVP from their phones. O'Connor also wants reviews to play a bigger role in what people discover. She says reviews of a host's events can affect how those events perform in the feed instead of simply sitting on a profile.
There is something almost funny about the concept. You open another social-style app because you want to spend less of your social life inside apps. But maybe that is exactly the point.
EXPERTS REVEAL WHY 'NONNAMAXXING' TREND MAY IMPROVE MENTAL, PHYSICAL HEALTH
NewTree Social founder Maddy O'Connor is shown with the app, which she created to help people discover local events and spend more time connecting in person. (NewTree)
How NewTree says it is different
NewTree is entering a crowded space. Meetup, Eventbrite and Facebook already help people discover events nearby, and both Meetup and Eventbrite offer personalized recommendations.

So what is NewTree trying to do differently? O'Connor says she wants the experience to feel more like a social platform built specifically around getting people together in person. She also says reviews can influence how a host's events perform in the feed, so better-reviewed experiences can potentially receive greater visibility. During NewTree's early pilot, O'Connor is personally reviewing and approving hosts before their events can appear publicly.

None of those ideas completely reinvents event discovery. The bet is that putting them together in a more curated, community-focused experience will give people another useful way to find things to do and meet people nearby. Whether that gives people enough reason to add NewTree to the apps they already use is one of the biggest things the company still has to prove.
The real test starts after you close the app

Here is what I would be watching. Does NewTree help people make plans they actually follow through on? Getting someone to download an app is one thing. Getting them to put on shoes, leave home and show up somewhere is much harder.
The idea works if you spend a few minutes browsing NewTree, find something interesting and eventually put the phone back in your pocket because you have somewhere to go.
It becomes a lot less interesting if people simply scroll through another feed filled with things they might someday do. O'Connor is very open about just how early NewTree is.

She told CyberGuy that NewTree is pre-traction and pre-revenue. Tampa Bay is the starting point because she wants to prove that people will use the platform in one market before trying to expand throughout Florida and eventually nationwide. So there is a long way to go. But the behavior NewTree is betting on already appears to be taking shape.
Safety has to follow you into the real world

Of course, using an app to find events where you may meet strangers brings some very real safety questions. O'Connor says she has taken a hands-on approach during NewTree's MVP stage. She told CyberGuy that she personally reviews and approves hosts before their events can appear on the platform. Users can report content or other users and block people. Hosts can also remove or report attendees.

NewTree's current support page says business profiles are reviewed before they can post. However, there is an important limitation. A verified badge means NewTree says it has confirmed that the business is who it claims to be. It does not mean NewTree is endorsing or guaranteeing a specific event.

NewTree's terms go further. They say events are generally operated independently by outside hosts and that NewTree does not ordinarily perform criminal background checks or identity verification on users, attendees, hosts or organizers.

So I would still do some homework before showing up at an unfamiliar event. Look up the organizer independently. Check the venue. If you are uncomfortable going alone, bring someone you trust. Technology can help you find people. It cannot remove all of the risks that come with meeting people you do not know.
What happens to your location?

Privacy deserves a close look too. O'Connor told CyberGuy that NewTree collects basic account information, including your name, email, date of birth and location. She says the app can use a saved profile location or, with your permission, your device location.

She also said the information is stored through NewTree's Supabase database, with database-level access controls designed to limit who can access different information. When someone RSVPs to a free event, O'Connor says the host receives the attendee's name, email and location information so they can manage and communicate with attendees.
1 IN 6 ADULTS PLAGUED BY LONELINESS AS RESEARCHERS REVEAL LASTING IMPACT OF COVID PANDEMIC
The NewTree app lets users browse nearby events, view host profiles and RSVP to activities that interest them. (NewTree)
There is also an age-rating wrinkle
Another detail could cause some confusion. Apple currently gives NewTree a 13+ age rating. NewTree itself says you must be at least 18 years old to create an account or use the platform.

O'Connor told CyberGuy that Apple's 13+ label reflects its content-based App Store rating rather than the minimum age NewTree allows on the platform. So, despite what you may see on the App Store listing, NewTree says the service itself is for adults 18 and older.
NewTree still has plenty to prove
Right now, Apple lists NewTree as an iPhone app. O'Connor told CyberGuy that Android support is planned but not available yet.

The business model is still taking shape too. O'Connor says she is leaning toward keeping the app free for users while eventually offering optional premium tools for businesses and hosts. Exactly what those paid features would include has not been decided.
So I would look at NewTree for what it is today: a very early app built around a much larger change in the way some people are thinking about technology.
What this means to you

Most of us could probably use a few more reasons to put the phone down and do something in the real world. Our phones have become where we communicate, work, watch videos and fill just about every empty moment.
Sometimes the screen starts taking the place of the experiences it was supposed to help us find. Maybe the better approach is expecting more from the technology we already use.

If an app helps you discover a local event, try something you would never have considered or meet someone you otherwise never would have crossed paths with, the phone becomes the starting point. Then it can get out of the way.
I like that idea. Use the technology to find something worth doing. Then look up from the screen and go do it.
Kurt's key takeaways

What stands out to me here is how good technology has become at keeping us looking down. Notifications pull us back in. Feeds always have something else waiting. Before you know it, another chunk of your day has disappeared into a screen. Now we are seeing signs that many people want something different. They still want technology, but they also want more opportunities to be around people in the real world. NewTree has a lot to prove. But I like the problem O'Connor is trying to solve. Your phone already knows how to keep you home and entertained for hours. Maybe the next really useful social app will be the one that gives you a good reason to leave.
Would you use an app designed to get you off your phone and out meeting people, or does downloading another social app defeat the whole purpose? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com.

title: 119,000 fake shops could steal your credit card details
summary: DoppelCart's 119,000 fake shopping domains steal credit card details at checkout, mimicking over 44,000 real brands with convincing cloned sites.
story: Halimah Delaine Prado, Google General Counsel, reveals the rise of AI-powered phishing scams originating from China's 'outsider enterprise.' She explains how these criminals use artificial intelligence to create highly convincing fake websites, impersonating trusted brands like T-Mobile to defraud hundreds of thousands of Americans, causing millions in losses. Prado highlights Google's strategy to combat these evolving threats.
You find a product you want for 65% off. The site looks polished, the branding feels familiar, and the deal seems hard to pass up. That could be exactly the trap.

Cybersecurity company Nebty has linked about 119,000 domains to a fake shopping operation called DoppelCart. The sites impersonate legitimate businesses and can steal payment details at checkout, including one-time bank verification codes.

BleepingComputer reports that more than 105,000 DoppelCart shops were active in Nebty's latest scans, while Nebty says the majority of the cluster remains online. So, before you jump on a huge discount from a store you do not recognize, take a closer look at who is really behind the checkout page.
FAKE RENTAL LISTING SCAMS CAN COST YOU THOUSANDS
Before entering payment information into an online storefront, check the web address and make sure the retailer is one you recognize and trust. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
NEW! 🩺 Free CyberGuy LIVE class: Get Better Healthcare With AI Saturday, September 26 at 11 a.m. ET / 8 a.m. PT

Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will show you five practical ways AI can help you organize your health history, remember important appointment details, understand complicated medical information, research prescriptions and prepare smarter questions for your doctor. No technical experience is needed.
Save your free spot at CyberGuyLive.com.
What is DoppelCart?

Nebty discovered DoppelCart while investigating fake shops that targeted several of its customers. Researchers noticed that stores impersonating different companies shared technical characteristics. They began following those connections through publicly available website scans.

The investigation eventually grew to roughly 119,000 associated domains. Nebty says that, to its knowledge, DoppelCart represents the largest publicly documented fake-shop cluster when measured by associated domains.
The company also makes an important point about attribution. Shared infrastructure does not prove that one person or organization controls every DoppelCart store.
Even so, the technical overlap is striking. Nebty CEO Benedikt Scheungraber told BleepingComputer that 96% of the confirmed shops shared identical build files and resolved to 27 commerce backends.
DoppelCart has swallowed a huge piece of the .shop domain

Most of the domains connected to DoppelCart use the .shop top-level domain. Nebty's September 2026 data included 118,787 distinct .shop domains linked to the cluster out of 4,361,908 .shop domains in the company's snapshot. That's 2.72%, or roughly one out of every 37 domains in that particular data set.

However, that number needs some context. Nebty says the snapshot represents domains listed in the .shop DNS zone. It does not tell us how many legitimate or fraudulent stores were operating at the same moment.

For comparison, researchers previously documented BogusBazaar, a fake-shop operation involving more than 75,000 domains. Nebty cautions that observation periods and counting methods differ between investigations, so the numbers are not perfectly comparable.
We reached out to GMO Registry, which operates the .shop domain, for comment but did not hear back before our deadline.
Why DoppelCart fake shops can look so convincing

The days when every scam website looked like somebody threw it together in five minutes are long gone. DoppelCart sites can copy product catalogs from real companies along with descriptions, branding and other material.
In some cases, researchers found fake stores loading assets directly from the legitimate company's servers. That creates a real problem for shoppers.
You may recognize the brand. The products look right. Nothing on the page immediately screams scam because much of the material came from the real business in the first place.
Scheungraber says DoppelCart shops mimic 44,182 different brands, with a median of two clones for each brand.

Some brands received much more attention. Researchers found more than 30 shops apiece targeting companies including SodaStream, Velasca, CurrentBody, Daniel Wellington, Dreame, Horze, MOVA and SPARK PAWS.
That 65% discount can be the hook

This is where the scam can catch you. Most of us shop around before spending money online. Finding the same product at a dramatically lower price can feel like a great deal. DoppelCart stores take advantage of that reaction.
Researchers found fake shops advertising discounts as high as 65%. Of course, a steep discount does not automatically mean you're looking at a scam. Real stores run clearance sales every day.

Still, if you've never heard of the retailer and its price beats everyone else by a mile, spend another minute checking who you're buying from. CyberGuy has a full guide on the warning signs worth checking before buying from an unfamiliar website: Tips to help you tell if an online store is real or a scam.
'THE ODYSSEY' STREAMING SCAM COULD STEAL YOUR BANK INFO
DoppelCart checkout pages can capture card details and other personal information as shoppers enter it online. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
How DoppelCart fake shops steal your card details
The real danger starts when you decide to check out. Nebty tested several checkout pages tied to the DoppelCart cluster and found code collecting:
Card numbersExpiration datesSecurity codesCardholder namesEmail addressesPhone numbersPhysical addresses
Card numbers
Expiration dates
Security codes
Cardholder names
Email addresses
Phone numbers
Physical addresses

According to the researchers, those fields can be transmitted through WebSockets to command-and-control infrastructure in real time. So, an attacker may receive the information while you're still sitting on the checkout page.

The technique has similarities to web skimming, where malicious code captures payment information as a shopper types it into an online checkout page. We've previously broken down how that kind of attack works and why shoppers may see no obvious warning: Web skimming attacks target major payment networks.
Your one-time bank code can be captured too

This is the part I find especially concerning. Many of us have been trained to see a verification code from our bank as an extra layer of protection. DoppelCart can potentially turn that security step against you.

Nebty found that the checkout code can relay the one-time confirmation code issued by a victim's bank. Attackers may then try to use the code to get past protections surrounding a fraudulent transaction.
So, don't automatically enter a bank code simply because a checkout page asks for it. Read the bank's message carefully. Look at the merchant and transaction details if they're included.
If something does not match the purchase you're making, stop the transaction and contact your bank through its official app or the number printed on your card.
The legitimate business can get dragged into the scam
DoppelCart creates another headache after the purchase. Some fake shops display the real company's legitimate customer support address.
Now imagine you place an order and nothing arrives. You find the support information on the site and contact the business demanding to know where your purchase went.

The company you're calling may have no idea what you're talking about because you never bought anything from it. Nebty says legitimate businesses have received complaints from shoppers over orders those businesses never processed.
The scammer gets the payment information. Meanwhile, the legitimate company gets the angry customer and has to explain that somebody copied its store.

Nebty says it tried to contact the main hosting provider associated with DoppelCart sites but received no response. Want to see whether a brand or website appears in the DoppelCart investigation? Search Nebty's DoppelCart database at investigations.nebty-id.com/doppelcart.
APPLE PAY TEXT SCAM THREATENS $8,250 LOSS IN 35 MINUTES
Fake online stores can copy legitimate product pages and branding, making it harder to tell when you are shopping on a scam site. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
How to spot a fake online store before you pay
A professional-looking site no longer gives you enough information to decide whether a retailer deserves your trust. Instead, slow down when you're shopping somewhere unfamiliar.

Look at the domain in your browser before entering payment information. A fake site may use a recognizable company name inside a completely different domain. If you're trying to buy directly from a well-known brand, find its official website independently. Also, don't let the padlock or HTTPS fool you. HTTPS tells you a website encrypts the connection. It does not prove the seller behind the site is legitimate. Scammers can encrypt websites too.

A 65% discount can make you want to buy before the deal disappears. That's when I would slow down. Check the product on the company's official website or compare it with a retailer you already know. If the price difference looks unusually large, investigate the seller.

Search the store's name before buying. Look beyond reviews displayed on the website itself. Search for independent complaints or reports that connect the domain to scams. Then check the company's contact information. A cloned website can look impressive while having very little legitimate history behind it.

The Federal Trade Commission recommends paying by credit card when possible for online purchases because credit cards provide protections when a transaction goes wrong. Some issuers also let you use virtual card numbers for online purchases. Availability varies by issuer. A virtual number can keep your primary card number away from the merchant and may let you shut down the virtual number if something goes wrong.

Don't treat a one-time verification code as a routine box to fill in. Read the message your bank sends. If the merchant or transaction looks unfamiliar, do not enter the code. Contact your card issuer through a trusted channel instead.

Check whether your bank or card issuer lets you receive notifications when purchases hit your account. Alerts can help you spot an unfamiliar transaction quickly. Do not ignore a small charge simply because the amount looks harmless. Any transaction you don't recognize deserves a closer look.

Strong antivirus software can help warn you about known malicious websites and dangerous links. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android & iOS devices at Cyberguy.com
However, no program catches every newly created fake shopping site. That means your own judgment still plays an important role when a store you've never heard of suddenly offers the deal of the year.
What to do if you already entered your card on a suspicious shop
Act quickly if you think you purchased from a DoppelCart site or another fake retailer. The FTC recommends contacting the financial institution you used to make the payment as soon as possible.

Use the number on the back of your card, your bank's official app or its official website. Tell the issuer that you entered your card information on a suspected fraudulent website. Ask whether the card should be locked or replaced with a new number. If you also entered a one-time verification code from your bank, tell them that too.

Review your recent transactions and continue watching the account. If you paid the fake retailer, tell your issuer that you believe the transaction involved a scam. Also report any other charges you do not recognize. The FTC recommends asking the card issuer or bank whether it can reverse the fraudulent transaction and return your money.

If the fake store asked you to create an account and you reused a password from somewhere else, change that password on the other accounts. Give important accounts unique passwords. A password manager can help generate and store strong passwords without forcing you to remember every one.

Remember what DoppelCart checkout pages can collect. The people behind the operation may have your contact information along with payment details. Be suspicious of unexpected bank warnings, delivery messages or refund offers connected to the purchase. Scammers sometimes target people who already lost money and then pose as someone who can help recover it. Go directly to your bank or the company's official website rather than clicking a link in an unexpected message.

If you downloaded a file, installed software or gave the suspicious site additional access to your device, update your security software and run a scan with strong antivirus software. If all you did was type card information into the fake checkout, focus first on protecting the payment account and watching for fraudulent transactions.
Report suspected fraud to the Federal Trade Commission at ReportFraud.ftc.gov. Reports can help authorities identify fraud patterns and investigate scam operations.
Kurt's key takeaways

What bothers me most about DoppelCart is how convincing these fake stores can look. You may recognize the products and the branding because scammers copied them from a real business. For me, that changes how I look at a bargain from a store I don't know. If the price seems unusually low, I want to know exactly who I'm buying from before I enter my card information. Take a minute to check the web address and search for the retailer on your own. That small pause could save you from having to replace your card or deal with fraudulent charges later.
Have you ever landed on an online store that looked completely legitimate but something made you suspicious, and what tipped you off? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com.

title: Iowa teacher, 10-year-old student die during fifth-grade school field trip at Lake MacBride State Park
summary: A fifth-grade field trip to Lake MacBride State Park turned fatal as authorities recovered two victims from waters near the Coralville Reservoir spillway.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.
An Iowa teacher and 10-year-old student died after an incident at Lake MacBride State Park during a fifth-grade school trip, authorities and school officials said.
The Johnson County Sheriff’s Office identified the victims Wednesday as Hannah Jorgensen, 24, of Tiffin, and Ahmed Osman, 10, of Iowa City.
The sheriff’s office said deputies responded shortly after noon Tuesday to a report of people in the water at Lake MacBride State Park near the Coralville Reservoir spillway.
Hannah Jorgensen, 24, was found dead in a body of water during a school field trip. (Hannah Jorgensen / Facebook)
GEORGIA TEACHER, FATHER HAILED AS HERO AFTER DYING TO SAVE GIRL FROM MYRTLE BEACH RIP CURRENT
At 12:43 p.m., first responders recovered an adult from the Coralville Reservoir. The victim was pronounced dead at the scene.
Authorities searched throughout the evening for a missing juvenile before suspending recovery efforts overnight.
Kayakers paddle at Lake Macbride State Park in Johnson County, Iowa, on May 25, 2020. (USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect)
The sheriff's office said the search resumed Wednesday, and first responders recovered the juvenile from the water at 1:24 p.m.
The Iowa City Community School District said Jorgensen was a fifth-grade teacher at Borlaug Elementary and Ahmed was a fifth-grade student at the school.
2 CUSTODIANS DEAD IN POSSIBLE MURDER-SUICIDE AT CHICAGO ELEMENTARY SCHOOL
Hannah Jorgensen, a fifth-grade teacher, was found dead at a reservior while on a class trip. (Hannah Jorgensen / Facebook)
The district said the deaths occurred during a School of the Wild field trip at the MacBride Nature Recreation Area.
The district said in a statement that it was "heartbroken" by the deaths.

Hannah Jorgensen, 24, a fifth-grade teacher at Borlaug Elementary in Iowa, was found dead. (Hannah Jorgensen / Facebook)

title: Hayden Panettiere's overdose shows fentanyl crisis 'doesn't discriminate,' Stanford psychiatrist says
summary: Hayden Panettiere's fatal fentanyl overdose involved a lethal mix of opioids, benzodiazepines and quetiapine, a Stanford addiction expert says.
story: In the wake of Hayden Panettiere's accidental overdose, Stanford addiction medicine specialist Dr. Anna Lembke explains fentanyl's dangers, the risks of mixing medications and why today's drug supply is more dangerous than ever.
Hayden Panettiere's fatal overdose is a stark reminder that the fentanyl crisis has not gone away, even as the United States makes genuine progress in reducing overdose deaths since peaking in 2022.
This week, the Greenville County Coroner's Office ruled that Panettiere died from the toxic effects of five drugs found in her system: fentanyl, 4-ANPP, Alprazolam, Methocarbamol and Quetiapine.

Dr. Anna Lembke, a Stanford psychiatrist and addiction medicine specialist, told Fox News Digital that while the circumstances surrounding the actress' death remain unclear, the combination of drugs in her system likely increased the risk of a fatal overdose.

"We don't know if she sought out fentanyl. We don't know if she had a counterfeit pill that had fentanyl in it. She might have been prescribed fentanyl for pain," Lembke said. "She was also on a benzo. We know combining benzos and opioids increases the risk of overdose of each of those medications separately. It looks like she was also on Quetiapine, a mood stabilizer, but also highly sedating in the mix."
Hayden Panettiere discusses "Nashville" with the Build Series at AOL HQ on Jan. 5, 2017, in New York City. (Roy Rochlin/FilmMagic)
HAYDEN PANETTIERE DEATH: DEA JOINS PROBE INTO WHAT HAPPENED TO LATE STAR
Lembke continued: "We don't know where she sourced it, but it does look like it was a lethal polypharmacy, including fentanyl, which on its own is an incredibly lethal drug."
The Cleveland Clinic defines polypharmacy as taking several medicines regularly, usually four or more.

While Lembke cautioned against drawing firm conclusions about what exactly led up to Panettiere's death, she said the tragedy underscores a broader reality: fentanyl remains a deadly threat that can affect anyone.

"This is still a very serious risk, and it's a risk that doesn't discriminate. Old and young, rich and poor, famous, not famous. Because of the increased access to these highly potent and potentially lethal drugs in the modern age, we're really all at risk for this problem," Lembke said.
Fentanyl, a synthetic opioid up to 50 times more potent than heroin, has transformed the nation's illicit drug supply over the past decade.
Pills containing fentanyl are displayed at the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) Northeast Regional Laboratory for testing in New York, on May 7, 2026. (Angela Weiss/AFP via Getty Images)
PRESLEY GERBER’S DEATH SPARKS QUESTIONS ABOUT OVERDOSE, WITHDRAWAL AND REHAB SAFETY
Deaths involving synthetic opioids, primarily illicitly manufactured fentanyl, began climbing sharply in 2014 and reached a record 73,838 in 2022, according to the National Institute on Drug Abuse.

Fentanyl's potency is only part of what makes it so dangerous, Lembke said. Just as concerning is how trace amounts are concealed in counterfeit pills designed to look like legitimate prescription medications.

Lembke said a "very real risk" for young people, even those who aren't struggling with addiction, is that they're given a pill at a party that looks just like Xanax or Oxycontin, when it is in fact a counterfeit pill that contains a small amount of fentanyl.
"A single dose to an opioid-naive person could kill, which is why it's so important that we have data-informed discussions with young people in particular," she said.
"The kind of experimentation with drugs in their youth that their parents might've engaged in relatively risk-free... it's not risk-free anymore" for young adults, she added.
Anna Lembke, a Stanford psychiatrist and author, gives a lecture on May 19, 2026, in Berlin, Germany. (Thomas Trutschel/Photothek via Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Lembke encouraged parents to get ahead of the issue by talking openly about drugs before their children encounter inaccurate or misleading information on social media.
If a parent or guardian recognizes their child has a substance-use disorder, Lembke said they should resist the impulse to brush it off as "normal teenage experimentation."

"These drugs are far too accessible and far too lethal to just leave it to hoping that it will be a passing phase the kid will outgrow," she said. "We know that the earlier we intervene with addiction-related problems, the more likely we are to reroute that person on a new path of life."
Lembke also offered a message to doctors, who she said should prescribe potentially addictive medications cautiously and closely monitor patients for signs of misuse.

As a practicing psychiatrist, Lembke routinely prescribes stimulants for ADHD, opioids for pain and benzodiazepines for insomnia and anxiety. But she said physicians have a responsibility to prescribe them in the lowest effective amounts for the shortest possible duration.

title: Ole Miss names students found dead as official addresses potential for foul play
summary: It remains unclear whether the deaths of Ole Miss students are connected, according to Lafayette County authorities.
story: Editor-in-Chief Regan Settle of Ole Miss's student-run news organization The Daily Mississippian, highlights growing student frustration after two campus drug overdose deaths, pressing university leaders to communicate directly.

OXFORD, Miss. — The two University of Mississippi students found dead under suspicious circumstances in recent days have been identified by the school — which also said the names were being released with their families' approval.
Robert Strang, a 20-year-old from Atlanta, is the older of the two victims. The second student was as Aidan Hamilton, an 18-year-old freshman from Colorado.

"We are heartbroken by the loss of our dear son and are trying to process this unimaginable loss," Strang's family spokesman Scott Sayres told Fox News Digital Thursday. "We are deeply grateful for the incredible outpouring of love, prayers and support by so many beloved friends and family. Their kindness has meant more to our family than we can ever express."
Both families have asked for privacy and compassion as they mourn the losses of their sons.
TWO OLE MISS STUDENTS FOUND DEAD AS PACKAGED KRATOM IS RECOVERED AT TWO SITES: OFFICIALS
Robert Strang pictured in an undated family photo. The 20-year-old University of Mississippi junior died under suspicious circumstances. (Strang family)

Separately, Commissioner of the Mississippi Department of Public Safety Sean Tindell told Fox News Digital that while authorities haven't uncovered any indications of foul play, they haven't ruled it out either.
"Until the autopsy is reported, and the investigators have an opportunity to get statements and collect evidence, then that final determination will not be made until later," he said.

Without the toxicology reports, it's also too early to determine whether kratom or other drugs were involved in the deaths. Police previously said that they found packages of kratom, which is commercially available in many places but not Lafayette County, at both scenes.

He also said that both deaths happened at around the same time, or at least within a few hours, which was also suspicious. However, he said he expects the autopsy reports to give investigators a more specific window.

"The timing of it is suspicious, but I don't know that they have any direct relation other than if they both had ingested the substance from the same source," he said. "Then at some point we would try to track it back to that source and take appropriate action."

Stewart Hall, a dorm building on the University of Mississippi campus where an 18-year-old student is believed to have died on Monday. Dispatch records show first responders arrived within a minute of being sent to the address. (Adam Sabes/Fox News Digital)
Social media posts from the Ole Miss chapter of the Phi Delta Theta fraternity identify Strang as one of seven co-chairmen of the 2026 Rush, when new members are recruited.

"As our university community continues to mourn the recent tragic loss of two of our students, I encourage everyone to remember that at the center of this are two grieving families, who are processing the unimaginable loss of a child," the school's Vice Chancellor for Student Affairs Dr. Shawnboda Mead said in a statement Thursday afternoon.

"We have been in touch with the families to offer our deepest sympathies and share university support and resources. Until now, we have upheld their wishes not to release the names of their students," she continued. "Today, the families of Aidan Hamilton, a freshman from Englewood, Colo., and Robert Strang, a junior from Atlanta, have given us permission to share their names. The families have asked for privacy as they grieve."
Mead continued to urge the public not to rely on speculation or unverified information about the case as law enforcement continues to investigate both deaths.

"We offer heartfelt condolences to the families, friends and classmates of Aidan and Robert," she said. "While there are no words that can alleviate the tremendous sorrow they are experiencing, please keep them close in your thoughts and prayers during this time of immense grief."

Authorities found packages of kratom, a commercially available drug that has been derided as "gas station heroin," at both scenes, however its role in either death was not immediately clear. Campus Greek life leaders have previously circulated a warning about a synthetic opioid called cychlorphine.

Cychlorphine can be treated with Narcan but sometimes requires multiple doses, students were told. It also may not show up on common drug-detecting strips used to find fentanyl contamination.

title: Texas triple murderer uses last words before execution to send message to death row inmates
summary: Ker'Sean Ramey received lethal injection at Huntsville prison, one week after accomplice LeJames Norman was executed for the same triple killing.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

A man convicted of murdering three people in their apartment while searching for drugs to steal was executed in Texas on Wednesday evening, a week after his accomplice was put to death for the same killings.
Ker'Sean Ramey, 41, died by lethal injection at the state penitentiary in Huntsville and was pronounced dead at 6:34 p.m. CDT, The Associated Press reported.
In the execution chamber, a prison chaplain rested his hand on Ramey's shoulder before leading him in a brief prayer. The warden then asked Ramey if he had any last words, the AP reported.
Ramey praised God and thanked his friends, family and fellow death row inmates, whom he called his brothers.
This photo provided by the Texas Department of Criminal Justice shows Ker'Sean Ramey on Oct. 31, 2022. (Texas Department of Criminal Justice via AP)
ARIZONA EXECUTES MAN WHO KILLED VICTIM BY DOUSING HIM IN GASOLINE AND SETTING HIM ON FIRE IN 2002 ATTACK

"To the brothers on Texas death row that grew up with me, that poured into me and showed what it means to be a man, because I came in young, and didn’t understand what manhood was... to you brothers... I greatly appreciate you," Ramey said moments before the injection was prepared.
As the pentobarbital took effect, Ramey took a deep breath, sputtered and began snoring. After 10 loud snores and two that were barely audible, he went still.
He was pronounced dead 14 minutes after the injection was first administered.
Ramey became the sixth inmate executed in Texas this year, with the state set to carry out three more lethal injections over the next two months.

In January 2007, Ramey was convicted and sentenced to death for the August 2005 shootings of Samuel Roberts, 24, Tiffani Peacock, 18, and Celso Lopez, 38, at a home they shared in Edna, a small rural city about 100 miles southwest of Houston.
The state of Texas execution chamber in Huntsville, Texas, is seen on May 27, 2008. (AP Photo/Pat Sullivan)
74-YEAR-OLD BECOMES FLORIDA'S OLDEST INMATE EXECUTED AFTER 1982 KILLING OF TEEN
LeJames Norman, Ramey's accomplice, lived across the street from the house and the two came to believe there was cocaine there, according to court records.
On Aug. 24, 2005, the men walked over to the home while wearing masks and knocked on the door. After Lopez answered the door, they forced their way inside, records show.

After finding no drugs, the two men fatally shot Lopez, then killed Peacock and Roberts when they arrived at the home. Before fleeing for good, Ramey returned and shot the victims again to ensure they were dead, according to court documents.
Norman was executed on Sept. 16 at the Huntsville prison, where all executions are carried out in Texas.
The Huntsville Unit prison is seen in Huntsville, Texas, on Sept. 14, 2024. (Francois Picard/AFP)
MANHATTAN PROSTITUTE PLEADS GUILTY TO KILLING 3 MEN WITH FENTANYL-LACED DRUGS IN ROBBERY SCHEME

Hours before Ramey was put to death, the Supreme Court rejected his final appeal. Ramey's attorneys argued jurors never heard mitigating evidence about his upbringing, including that he endured physical abuse as a child and grew up in poverty.
State prosecutors urged the Supreme Court to reject the appeal, calling it "meritless" and arguing the record showed Ramey had exhibited an escalating pattern of criminal behavior.

Norman was arrested about five months after the killings while attempting to re-enter the United States from Mexico, where he had fled. During Ramey's January 2007 trial, Norman testified that both men took part in the shootings, while Ramey's attorneys argued Norman was solely responsible.
This photo provided by the Texas Department of Criminal Justice shows LeJames Norman on Feb. 28, 2024. (Texas Department of Criminal Justice via AP)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Ramey's former girlfriend testified that she was with him when he threw two handguns into a lake after the killings and that he later gave her a detailed account of his role in the crime.
Norman pleaded guilty to capital murder and was sentenced to death in December 2008.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: Mistress says she gave ‘American Idol’ contestant ultimatum before wife’s killing blew up affair
summary: Caleb Flynn's mistress testified he talked about wanting Ashley Flynn dead and once said he was thinking about ways to kill her before the shooting.
story: Testimony continues as Flynn stands accused of fatally shooting his wife, Ashley, in February.

Former "American Idol" contestant Caleb Flynn told his mistress he stayed up until 4 a.m. "literally thinking of ways to kill" his wife and "not go to jail," one of a series of messages read to jurors Thursday in his Ohio murder trial.
Alleigha Botner returned to the witness stand for a second day and walked jurors through months of messages in which Flynn allegedly talked repeatedly about wanting Ashley Flynn dead or gone.
In one May 2025 message, Flynn allegedly wrote, "If I could literally kill her and not go to hell, I would do it in a heartbeat."
TEACHER FOUND DEAD WITH THROAT SLIT; DETECTIVES SCRUTINIZE HUSBAND’S SHIFTING STORY
Days later, he allegedly wrote, "I hate her, loathe her. I want her dead."

Caleb Flynn becomes emotional in court during his murder trial in Ohio. Flynn is accused of killing his wife, Ashley Flynn, in February 2026 and staging the scene to look like a break-in. (COURTESY: WKEF)
The messages became even more explicit in June, when Flynn allegedly told Botner, "Please hire someone to take [her] out. I need you in my life, I need you."
Botner responded: "So tempting. I can't live without you. And I've had this thought so often lately. How do we figure this out?"
TEEN PLANNED MIDDLE SCHOOL MASSACRE BEFORE MAKING DEADLY ‘LAST-MINUTE CHOICE’ TO KILL MOM: OFFICIAL
Botner later became emotional before reading one of her own messages aloud.
"I want to kill her, Caleb," Botner wrote.

Alleigha Botner testifies Wednesday in the Ohio murder trial of former "American Idol" contestant Caleb Flynn. Prosecutors say Botner had an affair with Flynn before his wife, Ashley Flynn, was killed. (CREDIT: WKEF)
Flynn allegedly responded: "That makes two of us."

Flynn is accused of fatally shooting Ashley in the back of the head inside their home Feb. 16 before staging the scene to look like an intruder had broken in. He has pleaded not guilty to aggravated murder and other charges.
Botner had prefaced the message by telling jurors, "I just wish I didn't say this."
In the same August exchange, Flynn allegedly went on to write that he had been "literally trying to find a way to get rid of her, to be rid of her."
Botner responded that she was "not asking that you take her life, obviously," but said getting a divorce "would change everything."
OHIO MAN CONVICTED AFTER TRYING TO SHOOT EX-WIFE AT POINT-BLANK RANGE INSIDE RESTAURANT IN CHILLING VIDEO

Botner also testified Flynn once showed her a gun he kept in the center console of his truck, though she could not remember what it looked like. Investigators have never recovered the weapon prosecutors allege Flynn used to kill Ashley.
Caleb Flynn in a 2013 "American Idol" Hometown Interview. Caleb is the husband of Ashley Flynn, who was shot and killed in her Ohio home on Monday, February 16, 2026. (YouTube/American Idol)
Jurors also heard that Flynn and Botner routinely deleted messages throughout their relationship.
MICROSOFT EXEC'S GRIEVING WIDOW FACES MAN ACCUSED OF PLOTTING HIS MURDER AS SHE REVEALS EERIE FINAL CALL
Asked when she advised Flynn how to delete data from his devices, Botner responded, "Multiple times."
"One of them being the night before Ashley was murdered," she testified.
Ashley and Caleb Flynn in an undated photo with their two children. (GoFundMe)

Botner also testified that on the night before Ashley's killing, she used ChatGPT to research whether messages documenting the affair could be permanently deleted and sent Flynn screenshots of the results.

She told jurors she feared the affair could surface during a divorce and cost her her job. Prosecutors established that Botner sent the screenshots about 5:47 p.m. Feb. 15, hours before Ashley was killed.
CALIFORNIA MOM BEGGED FOR HELP BEFORE EX GUNNED HER DOWN IN FRONT OF THEIR 4-YEAR-OLD SON: DA
Caleb and Ashley Flynn are pictured in an undated photo. (Ashley Flynn/Facebook)
SPURNED SPOUSES CASH IN AS NORTH CAROLINA’S 'HOMEWRECKER' LAW TURNS CHEATING INTO A COURTROOM JACKPOT
The two exchanged roughly 107,000 messages while routinely deleting their conversations.
By January, Botner testified, she had grown tired of waiting and gave Flynn a final deadline: leave Ashley by Jan. 11, or she would move on with her life and end their relationship.
FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X
Flynn did not leave, and Botner stopped communicating with him until Feb. 14 – Valentine's Day and two days before Ashley was killed.
Ashley Flynn, a Tipp City Schools substitute teacher and volleyball coach, was found dead in her Ohio home. (Tipp City Schools)
That day, she testified, Flynn told her he was "filing [for divorce] from Ashley" and was "actually leaving her this time."
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE
The night before Ashley was killed, Flynn and Botner discussed his plans for the following day, including telling family members about the divorce and obtaining a burner phone.
After Botner suggested he get the burner first, Flynn allegedly wrote, "I think I should pay cash for this so it's not in my bank account."
FLORIDA PLASTIC SURGEON ACCUSED OF KILLING ATTORNEY IN HIS OFFICE DEFENDS HIMSELF IN MURDER TRIAL
Shortly after midnight, Flynn allegedly told her, "It's happening, Ilya."
Then came another message: "February 16th day I'll never forget."
GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL
Caleb Flynn, 49, was arraigned in court on Friday, Feb. 20. (Dayton Daily News)
Botner responded, "You're about to be free."
SUSPECT IN MICROSOFT EXECUTIVE JARED BRIDEGAN'S MURDER CONVICTED IN ROADSIDE AMBUSH
Flynn replied, "I choose you."
Botner testified those were the final messages Flynn sent her before she learned Ashley had been killed.
At 7:50 a.m., Botner testified she sent Flynn her burner-phone number and told him to contact her there once he obtained his own burner. She later deleted the message.

Caleb Flynn appears in Miami County Common Pleas Court, Troy, Ohio, Monday, March 30, 2026. Flynn is charged with the murder of his wife, 37-year-old Ashley Flynn who was shot to death in their Tipp City home in February. (Matthew Symons for Fox News Digital)
Botner instead learned of Ashley's death after a fellow church congregant sent her a news story that morning.
"My heart started pounding," Botner testified. "It just seemed like too much of a coincidence that the day he's divorcing her, she's just dead all of a sudden."
Botner then messaged Flynn: "What is going on right now? Were you behind this?"
She testified she later deleted the message.
SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS
Botner later saw Flynn at Ashley's parents' home, where family members and church staff had gathered after the killing.
"The first thing he said to me was, ‘It didn't happen the way we thought it would, did it?'" Botner testified.

Botner said she became "very suspicious" and questioned Flynn about what happened. She testified Flynn told her he had been sleeping on the couch before waking to a gunshot and finding "blood everywhere" in Ashley's bedroom.
SEND US A TIP
Botner admitted Wednesday that she initially lied to the FBI about her relationship with Flynn when investigators interviewed her days after the killing.

"I was selfishly afraid that my reputation was going to be ruined and that I was going to lose my job," she testified. "And now that there was a murder attached, I didn't want to be attached to that in any way."
She began revealing more about the relationship after investigators told her they had found text messages on Ashley’s phone, Botner testified.
GOT A TIP?
Josh Ritter, a former prosecutor, criminal defense attorney and Fox News contributor, said Botner's testimony gives prosecutors evidence of motive.
"Motive. She provides motive," Ritter told Fox News Digital. "She gives jurors a reason for why would this man murder his wife."
Ritter said the significance goes beyond Flynn expressing frustration with his marriage or wanting a divorce.

"It's the idea that he's even discussing her being dead," Ritter said. "He went as far as to saying I literally would kill her. That's far beyond someone voicing their frustrations and venting to a lover."
LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

But Ritter said Flynn's attorneys can argue prosecutors cherry-picked the most damaging language from more than 100,000 messages and that Flynn was talking about leaving Ashley, not killing her, when he discussed what would happen Feb. 16.
The defense can also emphasize that investigators never recovered the alleged murder weapon, there was no eyewitness to the killing and no gunshot residue was found on Flynn, Ritter said.
"In an ideal world, would the prosecution want the murder weapon? Sure," Ritter said. "But ... it's something that the defense is obviously going to lean into."
Prosecutors asked Botner how she feels about Flynn today, and she said, "I hate him."

When asked why, Botner responded, "Because I believe that he murdered his wife."

Fox News Digital reached out to Flynn's attorney. Prosecutors finished their direct examination of Botner shortly before Thursday's lunch break, with the defense set to begin cross-examination when court resumes.

OXFORD, Miss. – An Ole Miss student says she was drugged at a bar over the weekend, days before two students were found dead, as bars around Oxford tighten security with fears running rampant through the college town.

Lafayette County Metro Narcotics said in a news release that investigators are looking into the deaths of two college-aged individuals whose bodies were discovered at separate locations. Fans enjoy tailgating before the Mississippi Rebels play the LSU Tigers at The Grove near Vaught-Hemingway Stadium in Oxford, Miss., on Sept. 30, 2023. (Getty Images)

"Later into that night, around the time when the game ended, I do not remember a single thing. And I was told by a boy that was there that I fell down," Harvey said.
