"We have provided comprehensive information to all employees and encourage them to consult a doctor if they experience any symptoms," the firm said.
Louis Casiano is a reporter for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to louis.casiano@fox.com.

title: China firm gave Iran lifeline to collect Hormuz tolls before pulling plug amid US warning
summary: After briefly issuing a web security certificate for a portal linked to Iran's U.S.-sanctioned Persian Gulf Strait Authority, a Shanghai-based firm revoked it, though the move could still draw scrutiny under U.S. sanctions rules
story: Lawyer and former OFAC official Jeremy Paner says even limited services to sanctioned Iranian entities could trigger sanction action.

Iran’s sanctioned Persian Gulf Straits Authority (PGSA) regained secure online access for four days after a Shanghai-based internet security firm provided and then revoked its web credentials, enabling Tehran to vet vessels, collect Strait of Hormuz tolls and operate despite U.S. digital restrictions, global internet monitors said.

TrustAsia issued an automated domain-validated certificate, a routine process that verifies control of a website domain through server checks and typically does not involve manual vetting or background checks.

The move prompted U.S. sanctions experts, including Jeremy Paner, a partner at Hughes Hubbard & Reed, to urge TrustAsia to review its compliance program before offering further services to the IRGC-linked maritime authority — with Paner warning them to act "before it is too late."
The PGSA first said its website was disrupted Aug. 10 because of "the enemy's political influence on the internet service provision systems," according to a post on X.
IRAN REQUESTS TALKS WITH US AS WHITE HOUSE WARNS 'VIOLENCE WILL BE MET WITH VIOLENCE'
Oil tankers and cargo ships line up in the Strait of Hormuz as seen from Mina Al Fajer, United Arab Emirates, Wednesday, March 11, 2026. (Altaf Qadri/AP Photo)

NetBlocks CEO Alp Toker told Fox News Digital that the authority had lost its web security credentials after the entity was added to the U.S. Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) sanctions list on May 27.

The loss of standard SSL/TLS certificates, Toker said, made the PGSA website inaccessible using standard browsers. This forced shipping firms to use unencrypted connections that, according to Toker, could leave their data vulnerable to interception.

While no data breaches resulting from the use of these connections have been made known, and there are no known instances in which a shipping firm’s data was intercepted and used to its detriment because of the certificate expiration, Toker said the site’s inaccessibility resulted in a shift to what he described as "insecure protocols."
"The digital transparency records are authoritative on this," he said, adding that the measure forced the traffic into a format that could be readily intercepted.
"This is a class of vulnerability open to government exploitation, rather than a corporate breach or personal data leak."
Toker claimed this could make it easier for authorities to read communications sent through the platform, potentially identifying shipping firms collaborating with the PGSA.
TRUMP SAYS IRAN WILL PAY — WHAT IT TAKES TO END THE WAR REMAINS UNCLEAR

Naval units from Iran and Russia simulate the rescue of a hijacked vessel during joint drills at the Port of Bandar Abbas in Hormozgan, Iran, on Feb. 19, 2026. (Iranian Army/Handout/Anadolu via Getty Images)

"The net result was that the website was more difficult to access, because most web browsers strongly encourage the use of secure HTTPS," Toker said, adding that any form submissions could have been easily "eavesdropped on because they're no longer encrypted in transit."

"The mentioned issue has been resolved, and the secure domain https://pgsa.ir is now once again available for submitting requests using any browser," the PGSA said six days later on Aug. 17 and in another post shared on X.
"If the issue recurs in the future, the HTTP domain will again be temporarily available using the Firefox browser."

Toker confirmed that Iran had turned to Shanghai-based certificate authority TrustAsia Technologies, which he said issued new digital security credentials to the PGSA despite the U.S. sanctions, restoring secure access to its website.

"Iran’s IRGC extorts vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz through the so-called Persian Gulf Strait Authority," the Treasury Department said in May when designating the entity, adding that the PGSA "spearheads an Iranian-controlled scheme that flagrantly violates international law and U.S. sanctions."

"Anyone cooperating with the so-called strait authority may be providing support to and receiving services from the IRGC, which ultimately benefits from this attempted extortion, and may therefore be exposed to sanctions risk," the Treasury Department warned.
The Chinese firm bills itself as a "leading and professionally certified certification authority in China with its focus on trusted, secure and cryptographic communications in the digital world."
Its mission, it says, is to "Build trust everywhere in the digital world."
"Almost all of these root authorities do business with the U.S., so they tend to comply with U.S. sanctions," Toker said.
But TrustAsia, he noted, had "gone its own way, building a China-first certificate infrastructure that sidesteps the West."
Toker said TrustAsia had "simply gone ahead and issued Iran's PGSA with a new certificate, and Iran was once again collecting revenue from ships passing the Strait via its secure online portal."
TRUMP CALLS ON ARAB NATIONS TO SIGN ABRAHAM ACCORDS

The Treasury Building is viewed in Washington, May 4, 2021. The U.S. on Wednesday imposed a new round of sanctions on a group of 20 people and firms allegedly involved in a financial facilitation network for the benefit of the Iranian military. The Treasury Department sanctions impact firms and people spanning from Hong Kong to the United Arab Emirates. (AP Photo/Patrick Semansky)
Paner warned that U.S. authorities would have enforcement powers over such actions.
"The U.S. has incredibly broad authority to impose sanctions on non-Iranian companies that provide any sorts of services to sanctioned Iranian companies," he told Fox News Digital.

"Many times, that authority will be abbreviated or explained as being providers of material support to sanctioned Iranian companies. But in fact, any level of services whatsoever could be the basis for the United States imposing sanctions against the company for providing services to Iran."
"Restoration of the certificate is unequivocally sanctionable," Paner warned.
"Restoring the certificate is/was a service provided to the PGSA, which can be the basis for imposing sanctions pursuant to Executive Order 13224, as amended.

"That authority does not in any way require that the service be ‘knowingly’ provided to the PGSA. In other words, the automated nature of the service is irrelevant and does not make the service any less sanctionable," the lawyer added.
In a statement to Fox News Digital on Aug. 20, a spokesperson for TrustAsia confirmed that the firm issued a "Domain Validated TLS certificate for pgsa.ir."
"Thank you for bringing this matter to our attention," the firm said before clarifying that "DV certificates are issued through automated validation of control over the requested domain names."
IRAN ACCELERATES EXECUTION CAMPAIGN AGAINST ANTI-REGIME ACTIVISTS AMID INTERNET CENSORSHIP
Iranian Navy soldiers on an armed speed boat in the Persian Gulf near the Strait of Hormuz. (Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
"This process does not verify or assert the legal identity, affiliation, or sanctions status of the entity operating or benefiting from the domain.

"As a result, the relationship described in your inquiry was not identified during the automated issuance process." Following the firm's review, TrustAsia said it "added the entire pgsa.ir domain namespace to our restricted-issuance list to prevent further issuance or renewal."
"We also expect to complete revocation of the existing certificate within this week," the spokesman said on Aug. 20.
These actions are precautionary compliance and risk-control measures. They should not be interpreted as a finding that the certificate was technically misissued, TrustAsia said.
Toker confirmed the TrustAsia certificate's privilege had been withdrawn on Aug. 21 at 12:15:25 UTC. "This usually means the issuer has taken action," he said.

The internet expert clarified that the revocation will gradually be coming into effect, with the firm "signaling that the PGSA certificate should no longer be trusted, and they're distributing this notice that privilege is withdrawn, usually meaning customer misuse or breached terms of use."
"The secure website will stop working in most browsers, unless the owners can find a certificate authority that's willing to issue a new certificate," Toker said.
IRAN’S UNSEEN SUPREME LEADER BECOMES WEAPON IN ESCALATING POWER STRUGGLE, EXPERTS SAY

Iran sanctions prompt capital flight as Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent reports Iranian leaders allegedly wired tens of millions overseas amid protest crackdowns. (Anna Moneymaker/Saeid Zareian/Picture Alliance via Getty Images)
After reviewing TrustAsia's statement, Paner also said that OFAC would expect the company to "use the discovery as an opportunity to enhance its compliance program before it is too late."
The former OFAC official clarified that Iran's revenue collection in the waterway would likely draw high-level scrutiny in Washington.
"Iran's attempt to extort the world in the movement of oil through the Strait of Hormuz is of the utmost importance to OFAC, which is the agency that implements and enforces U.S. economic sanctions."
Because major U.S. web browsers currently recognize TrustAsia’s root certificates, American systems would have automatically trusted the sanctioned Iranian portal.

Toker claimed the Treasury Department could have found TrustAsia in violation of sanctions for providing material assistance to a blocked entity, potentially forcing tech giants such as Google and Microsoft to revoke trust in TrustAsia.
There is no evidence that this process had begun or was likely to occur.
"This could have splintered the global chain of trust and potentially render much of the Chinese web inaccessible from the West," Toker warned.
IRAN IS NOT A NORMAL NATION YOU CAN MAKE DEALS WITH; IT’S A NATIONAL SECURITY THREAT

Ahmad Vahidi, commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Quds Force, Esmail Qaani, and Iraj Masjedi, deputy coordinator of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Quds Force, participate in a ceremony to mark the memory of former IRGC commander, Hossein Salami, who is killed in Israeli attacks, at a mosque in an IRGC organizational house complex in Tehran, Iran, July 25, 2025. (Morteza Nikoubazl/Nur Photo via Getty Images)
Paner clarified that the certificates authenticate the site, boosting its credibility, and suggested TrustAsia should have weighed the risks of working with sanctioned entities.
"There's always reputational risk involved in any company that decides to do business with the IRGC."
"If I were advising TrustAsia, I would at minimum immediately identify all other IRGC companies receiving services."
Paner added that this latest situation aligned with broader warnings from administration officials.

"I think this dovetails pretty nicely with Secretary Bessent's comments about how the coming sanctions are going to be unlike any that has come prior. Sanctions require a careful balancing of the costs and the benefits.
"When it's a Chinese tech company providing necessary services to the IRGC, I'm confident that the U.S. government is going to forego any sort of balancing in that regard."

The United States on Aug. 24 had sanctioned nearly 60 Iran-linked individuals, entities and vessels and expanded the threat of secondary sanctions, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said. These did not include TrustAsia.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Bessent described the measures as part of an "economic onslaught" targeting Tehran’s global financial networks under "Operation Economic Outcast."
A Chinese Embassy spokesperson also said in a statement: "I am not aware of the specifics you mentioned. I have no information to provide."
Fox News Digital reached out to the U.S. Department of the Treasury and the White House for comment.

Emma Bussey is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital. Before joining Fox, she worked at The Telegraph with the U.S. overnight team, across desks including foreign, politics, news, sport and culture.

title: ‘Voters get to choose — just not the result’: Russia’s parliamentary election reaches occupied Ukraine
summary: Russian State Duma elections will be held in occupied Donetsk, Luhansk, Kherson, and Zaporizhzhia amid accusations of armed voter intimidation.
story: FDD's Keti Korkiya says Russians are likely scared to give pollsters their real opinions on Putin and the war ahead of Friday's election.

Russian State Duma elections began Friday — the first since the invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Voting is also taking place in the areas annexed from Ukraine in the east as Putin looks to reinforce popular support for the war.
OSCE election observers are not invited to monitor the outcome of the elections, a telling signal, critics say, that the Kremlin has no intentions of conducting free and fair elections.

"Russia’s refusal to invite an election observation mission seriously breaches its international commitments and shows a worrying disregard for democratic standards. Election observation is not optional — it is something that all OSCE participating States have agreed to, and it is a cornerstone of transparency and accountability," OSCE Parliamentary Assembly President Pere Joan Pons told Fox News Digital.
Russian President Vladimir Putin holds a Security Council meeting in Moscow on Friday, Aug. 7, 2026. (Alexander Kazakov/Pool Sputnik Kremlin via AP)
Russia enacted strict censorship laws after the invasion, criminalizing any dissent about the operation or the armed forces and spreading misinformation about the war.
CIA DIRECTOR JOHN RATCLIFFE MET WITH RUSSIAN INTELLIGENCE OFFICIALS IN VISIT TO MOSCOW, KREMLIN SAYS

As the Kremlin has tried to keep popular support in favor of its war against Ukraine, a Russian court sentenced Lev Shlosberg, a vocal critic and leader of one of Russia’s only opposition parties to over 11 years in a penal colony for criticizing the war. Prior to Shlosberg’s sentencing, Russia's Supreme Court banned his opposition Yabloko Party from participating in September’s Duma elections.
There are nine parties on the list, all supportive of Putin, including the Kremlin's own United Party in the elections, The Associated Press reported.

Shortly after Russia’s invasion in 2022, Moscow unilaterally annexed portions of occupied Ukrainian territory in Donetsk, Luhansk, Kherson and Zaporizhzhia. In 2023, Russian President Vladimir Putin signed legislation allowing elections to take place in the occupied territories. Ukraine and the international community do not recognize Russian sovereignty over the occupied regions.

Elections in Russia, and by extension in the occupied territory, are seen by his critics as window-dressing opportunities used by Putin to highlight his narrative that the war in Ukraine and the annexation of Ukrainian territory was a legitimate and lawful action.

Keti Korkiya from the Foundation for Defense of Democracies Russia Program told Fox News Digital that, "Russians are ready to support, symbolically, Putin, the Kremlin and the war, but if they have to pay a personal price, or even [an] economic price, they are unwilling to do that. That's why Russia has not done another wave of mobilization."
Firefighters put out the fire in a multi-story apartment building following a Russian missile attack in Kharkiv, Ukraine, on Saturday, March 7, 2026. (Andrii Marienko/AP)
The upcoming elections, like most elections in Russia, will take place under a climate of pervasive fear and manipulation, not the freedom to exercise a democratic right, according to critics.
"It’s a total regime of terror," Jaroslava Barbieri, research fellow at the Ukraine Forum at Chatham House, told Fox News Digital.

The last time Russian elections were held in the occupied territories was in 2024, when Putin secured a fifth term in office, winning nearly 90% of the vote. Residents in occupied Ukraine were forced to acquire Russian passports, which is how authorities are able to compile lists of voters.
FORMER GEORGIAN PRIME MINISTER SAYS NATION'S ELECTION WAS 'RIGGED,' AND 'WRITTEN IN MOSCOW'
A woman casts her ballot at a mobile polling station during early voting in Russia's presidential election in Donetsk, Russian-occupied Ukraine, on March 14, 2024. (Stringer/AFP via Getty Images)

"Election officials are escorted by Russian soldiers carrying ballot boxes door-to-door. Ostensibly framed as a security measure against Ukrainian partisan strikes, this is about direct intimidation, and it is a flagrant violation of international law," Barbieri added.

President Vladimir Putin said in August that the State Duma elections will reaffirm Russia's stability on the world stage, noting the election will highlight the "maturity" of Russia’s political system and resilience in the face of foreign aggression, according to Turkey's Anadolu Agency.

Russia’s Central Election Commission (CEC) approved new electoral regulations that will be implemented in occupied Ukraine. The Commission stressed the importance of early and at-home voting to prevent large gatherings which could be exploited by Ukrainian attacks.

Russia's ministry of foreign affairs posted on X that preparations for overseas voting in Russia’s State Duma elections are nearly complete. It said there are 326 polling stations set up at Russian embassies and consulates in 152 countries.
Volodymyr Ariev, a member of the Ukrainian Parliament, said people living in temporarily occupied Ukrainian territories should boycott the staged Russian elections.

"Any sort of elections held in the temporarily occupied Ukrainian territories is illegal and a breach of international law. Ukraine will never recognize any person ‘elected’ as a member of Parliament in the temporarily occupied territories," Ariev told Fox News Digital.
Ariev said people living in the occupied east should leave their homes and spend election day someplace else, to avoid being coerced into voting.
PUTIN PLANS FOR NEXT 6-YEAR TERM AS RUSSIANS VOTE IN 'NEITHER FREE NOR FAIR ELECTION'

Ivana Stradner, who focuses on Russian information security and influence operations at the FDD, says as Russia’s battlefield momentum stalls, the costs of war mount, and Ukraine brings the conflict to Russia’s doorstep, Putin is seeking political legitimacy this election.

"The State Duma elections give the Kremlin a chance to manufacture the appearance of public support… not only for United Russia, but for continuing Putin’s aggression in Ukraine. When the battlefield gets harder to sell, the ballot box becomes another way to sell the war," Stradner told Fox News Digital.
A soldier fires a third-generation Javelin man-portable anti-tank missile system during a professional training session on Jan. 7, 2026, in Ukraine. (Ukrinform/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

In the 2024 presidential elections, the annexed Donetsk People’s Republic and Luhansk People’s Republic delivered well above the current targeted 70% support, voting well over 90% for President Putin.
"Apparently, in Putin’s version of democracy, the voters get to choose… just not the result," Stradner added. The three days of voting ends on September 20.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: Netanyahu takes the U.N. stage facing global isolation and a fight for his political future
summary: As Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu pleads his country’s case at the United Nations General Assembly, his target audience will likely be Israeli voters.
story: TEL AVIV — Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu pleaded his country’s case to the world at the United Nations General Assembly on Thursday before an audience of mostly empty seats.
But the audience Netanyahu was really trying to reach was closer to home: Israeli voters ahead of next month’s crucial elections.
As Netanyahu stepped up to the lectern, hundreds of diplomats showed their disdain for Israel’s bloody crackdown on Palestinians in Gaza by rising from their seats and walking out en masse.
Netanyahu responded with similar disdain. “If there are any more moral cowards who haven’t left the hall, please do so now,” he said.
Then Netanyahu went on to revisit Hamas’ attacks on Israel in October 2023 in which about 1,200 people were killed and which sparked the latest round of fighting.
Netanyahu also defended the ongoing war on Iran in existential terms. “If we hadn’t done it, we’d all be dead,” he said.
The prime minister thanked President Donald Trump for taking the side of Israel in what he called a “battle against the barbarians.”
And, as expected, he accused New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani of antisemitism and cozying up to what he said were his Hamas “buddies.”
“You can’t silence me,” he said, addressing Mamdani. “You can’t silence the truth.”

title: Bond yields surge to fresh two-decade highs but oil prices buffeted by Iran headlines
summary: Key U.S. Treasury yields surged to fresh two-decade highs Thursday, as the price of oil returned to $105 per barrel.
story: Key U.S. Treasury yields surged to fresh two-decade highs Thursday, as the price of oil jumped to as high as $108 per barrel.
The yield on the 30-year U.S. Treasury bond soared as high as 5.47%, a level not seen in 22 years.

After posting its biggest one-day rise since April 2025, the yield on the 10-year U.S. Treasury bond continued advancing on Thursday. In early trading it climbed as high as 5.18%. That remains its highest level since 2007.
Due to the influence that the 10-year yield has over consumer borrowing rates, the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate jumped to 7.37% on Thursday, its highest level since May 2024.

Meanwhile, oil prices jumped again overnight after a mediated U.S. dialogue with Iran at the United Nations General Assembly produced no tangible evidence of any progress toward ending the seven-month war.

Much of the day’s gains in oil were reversed shortly after midday Eastern time, following a Reuters report that U.S. and Iranian negotiators are exploring a phased path out of the war. The path reportedly involves Tehran reopening the Strait of Hormuz, according to Reuters’ multiple unnamed sources.
NBC News has not confirmed the Reuters report.
The reversal was short lived, however, and international Brent crude oil continued rising and closed higher by 3.4% at $106.60. U.S. crude oil ended the day higher by 2.6% at $94.61 per barrel.
Since the start of the year, both Brent and West Texas Intermediary crude are up more than 65%.

Those rising oil prices have continued to push commercial diesel fuel prices to all-time records. On Thursday, the national average price for diesel was $6.51, effectively unchanged from a day earlier, but up 73% since the Iran war began.
Likewise, the national average price of regular unleaded gas was 50% higher Thursday than it when the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran in late February, at $4.48 per gallon.

Stocks fell in early trading, but like oil, sharply reversed course on the Reuters report. The S&P 500 erased a drop of 0.5%, while the Nasdaq Composite erased a 0.9% slip. Both indexes were trading flat around 2 p.m. ET.
A global sell-off
Around the world, the bond sell-off is roiling sovereign debt markets.

“The acceleration higher in US rates yesterday is being felt globally as to highlight for the umpteenth time that we’re all in this global bond boat together,” wrote Peter Boockvar, chief investment officer at OnePoint BFG Wealth.
The yield on Japan’s 10-year bond rose to its highest level since 1996 on Thursday, while Germany’s 10-year bund notched its highest yield since 2009.
“As summer officially ends, macro data are still fairly solid in the US, as indicated by a 4%-type unemployment rate and 2%-ish growth,” wrote Bank of America’s global rates analysts.
“But the risks continue to pile up for anxious markets,” they added, pointing to ongoing trade wars, the energy supply shock, upcoming midterm elections and potential risks to the AI boom.

One major driver of the surge in bond yields this week was a report from S&P Global, released Wednesday morning, that found that while U.S. business activity accelerated in September, “firms’ input costs have meanwhile jumped in September at the steepest rate for four years, with fuel and transport costs spiking higher.”
That led investors and traders to ramp up their bets on Fed rate hikes.
Federal Reserve Bank of New York President John Williams said the central bank still has more work to do to help bring down inflation.
It’s “likely that another rate hike may be appropriate by the end of the year,” Williams said during a speech in London Thursday.
Nonetheless, he said, the U.S. economy has demonstrated “remarkable resilience” in the face of “significant shocks” hitting it.
Another key official, Anna Paulson, president of the Philadelphia Fed, said Thursday that she too expects “some modest further tightening may be warranted.”
In central banker parlance, tightening refers to raising rates.
Bessent’s next move
The rise in bond yields has continued despite a series of measures taken — and warnings delivered — by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent earlier this month.
“I am the house now,” Bessent said on Sept. 8, “and you can bet against me if you want.”

At the time, Bessent was defending a Treasury Department intervention to help prop up the Japanese yen. The hope was that a stronger yen would relieve pressure on the Japanese government to sell U.S. Treasury bonds.
But it hasn’t entirely worked, and as of Thursday, the Japanese yen had again weakened to levels on par with it’s exchange rate against the U.S. dollar from early September.
Bessent has also intervened in the U.S. bond markets, buying back longer-dated Treasurys in an effort to keep their yields low.
In response to the department’s initial buyback earlier this month, bond yields rose — exactly the opposite reaction from what the administration intended.
But Bessent has brushed off the stumble, insisting that the U.S. bond market is still the “best performing” in the world and crediting President Donald Trump for it.
“If some of the Bloomberg Terminal bros are unhappy with what I’m doing, well, that’s too bad,” Bessent said in an interview on Sept. 10.

The second round of Bessent’s buyback plan was conducted Thursday, when the Treasury bought back about $4 billion worth of 20- and 30-year bonds. As with the initial round, yields rose to their highest level of the session on the news —  but the jump was far less notable than it had been a month ago.

“Mechanically, today’s operation went more smoothly,” said Brian Rehling, co-head of of global fixed income strategy at Wells Fargo. But “long-end yields are still being set by inflation, Fed expectations,” and the volume of debt being issued.

“Today’s operation is unlikely to alter the trajectory of long-term interest rates, which we believe will continue to move higher until the market believes inflation is being brought under control,” he added.
“US Treasury Secretary ‘House’ Bessent seems to be demonstrating the house does not always win,” wrote Paul Donovan, the chief economist at UBS Global Wealth Management, on Thursday morning.
CORRECTION (Sept. 24, 2026, 2:19 p.m. ET): A previous version of this article misstated Thursday’s national average price for diesel. It was $6.51, not $4.51.

title: These young quarterbacks were supposed to break out. Now they’re hurt.
summary: The New York Giants’ Jaxson Dart on Monday became the latest upstart QB to be sidelined with an injury, joining the Bears’ Caleb Williams and the Commanders’ Jayden Daniels as signal callers who had to leave the field early in Week 2.
story: The New York Giants were one of the NFL’s pleasant surprises in Week 1, beginning the John Harbaugh era with an impressive win over the Dallas Cowboys thanks in large part to the play of second-year quarterback Jaxson Dart.

The Giants’ dreams of a turnaround season quickly hit a roadblock on Monday, however, as Dart became the latest upstart QB to be sidelined with an injury. And now Dart may miss the rest of the regular season after imaging on Tuesday revealed his knee was hurt worse than the team initially feared, according to multiple reports.
Only two weeks into the NFL season, several of the game’s young stars are seeing their seasons upended due to varying degrees of injuries.

Dart joined the Chicago Bears’ Caleb Williams and the Washington Commanders’ Jayden Daniels as signal callers who had to leave the field early in Week 2. That trio joined a list of sidelined quarterbacks that also includes the Minnesota Vikings’ Kyler Murray and the defending Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks’ Sam Darnold.
All five of those players are former first-round draft picks — and all are under the age of 30.

Dart left in the first quarter of New York’s 28-6 loss to the Los Angeles Rams. On a third-and-8 pass attempt, Dart was sandwiched by multiple players as the pocket collapsed around him, and he took a substantial hit to his left knee from a Rams linebacker.
Dart limped off the field and was taken back to the locker room. After initially being ruled questionable to return, he was ruled out for good in the second half.
“He’s going to be OK,” Giants general manager Joe Schoen told ESPN’s Laura Rutledge during the “Monday Night Football” broadcast, adding that Dart would undergo X-rays at the stadium.
Dart’s hard-charging play style raised eyebrows during his rookie season, when he missed time due to a concussion but seemingly refused to tone down his aggressiveness when he returned.
During the preseason, Dart even expressed confusion at why he so often is required to enter the blue medical tent on the sidelines.

“I really respect the rules, and the thought behind, you know, the NFL has of keeping players healthy and reviewing things,” Dart said in August after a big hit required he undergo a mandatory medical evaluation. “But at the same time, I’m still puzzled by just feeling like every time that I get hit, you know, I just find my way in there.”
Dart’s injury Monday, though, came on a relatively routine pass play, highlighting how no quarterback is ever truly safe.

The same can be said of the Commanders’ Daniels, who dislocated his left elbow while trying to regain his balance after he was tripped by one of his own lineman in a 37-20 loss to the Cowboys. Daniels, the 2024 Offensive Rookie of the Year, dislocated the same elbow last season, in which he appeared in only seven games due to multiple injuries.
“It sucks for him,” Washington coach Dan Quinn told reporters Monday. “I know how much these guys put into it. So, when there are setbacks like this, you just want to stand by them.”

A little before Daniels’ exit, the Bears’ Williams was carted off the field with a hamstring strain in a 9-3 loss to the Vikings. While Williams’ emotional exit from the game quickly became a social media meme, it also cut short what had been an exciting start to the season. Chicago was coming off a Week 1 in which it had scored 59 points.
“He’s right now working through every avenue that he’s got available to get back on track here. We’ll see what that looks like,” Bears coach Ben Johnson told reporters Monday.
Johnson added that Williams has an ability to recover quickly, and his injury is considered week-to-week.
While the Bears, Giants and the Commanders all lost after their starters went down, their seasons are far from over.
The Vikings lost Murray in Week 1 but still managed a 2-0 start to the season with Carson Wentz at the helm. And now Murray is expected to start in Week 3 after recovering from a concussion.

The Seahawks are also 2-0 with Drew Lock playing in place of Darnold, and even exploded for 31 points on Sunday. Darnold is expected to return to practice this week, though his starting status is up in the air.
For now, the Bears will turn to Tyler Bagent, the Giants to Jameis Winston, and the Commanders to Marcus Mariota as the three clubs try to keep their seasons afloat without their young leaders.

And Dart, Williams and Daniels — all three of whom have flashed potential to not only be great players but stewards for the league because of their exciting style of play — will have to wait a little longer to cement their star turns.

title: University of Mississippi identifies 2 students found dead in cases that raise kratom concerns
summary: The University of Mississippi named two undergrads, from Colorado and Georgia, as the students found dead in cases that sparked renewed concerns about kratom.
story: The University of Mississippi on Thursday named two undergrads, from Colorado and Georgia, as the students found dead earlier this week in cases that sparked renewed concerns about the drug kratom.
Aidan Hamilton, an 18-year-old freshman from Englewood, Colorado, and Robert Strang, a 20-year-old junior from Atlanta, died this week, Ole Miss said.

Both students were found on Monday, one on campus and the other in the city of Oxford, authorities have said. Packaged kratom was discovered during each of these separate death investigations, but no definitive link has been made between the drug and these deaths, officials said.

Kratom is an herb with opioid-like effects sometimes sold at gas stations or online. It has gained popularity in the U.S. as an unapproved treatment for pain, anxiety and drug dependence.  Kratom can either be stimulating or sedating, depending on the dosage taken, according to the Drug Enforcement Administration.
Shawnboda Mead, the vice chancellor for student affairs, urged the campus community to reserve any judgement until law enforcement finishes its probe.

“We know there is heightened media attention and that you may be eager for answers. We also recognize that inaccurate information is being shared by individuals who do not have access to the facts,” Mead said in statement.

“We can all help by not repeating information that has not been officially confirmed and by avoiding public speculation about what happened or why, especially as the causes of the two deaths are still under investigation.”
Phi Delta Theta identified Strang as a member of its fraternity.

“Out of respect for Robert, his family, and those closest to him, the Fraternity has refrained from public comment until his name was publicly released,” Phi Delta Theta said in a statement on Thursday.

“The loss of two young lives is a profound tragedy,” the fraternity said. “Phi Delta Theta joins the University of Mississippi and the broader Ole Miss community in mourning Robert and Aidan Hamilton and extending our deepest sympathies to their families, friends, chapter brothers, classmates, and all those who knew and loved them.”

title: Ex-boyfriend of former Sen. Kyrsten Sinema allegedly threw 22 of her paintings in a pool
summary: Former Arizona Sen. Kyrsten Sinema’s former bodyguard and romantic partner was arrested earlier this month in Maricopa County after allegedly breaking into her home and damaging $200,000 worth of artwork and expensive alcohol.
story: Former Arizona Sen. Kyrsten Sinema’s former bodyguard and romantic partner was arrested earlier this month in Maricopa County after allegedly breaking into her home and damaging $200,000 worth of artwork and expensive alcohol.

The incident took place on Aug. 30 while Sinema was out of town, according to charging documents. Matthew Ammel, 39, allegedly contacted Sinema and demanded that she post a video to her X account. He told her that if she declined to do so, he would damage a painting every 10 minutes, according to the documents.
Sinema told law enforcement officers that she refused, prompting Ammel to take down about 22 paintings and throw them into the swimming pool, according to a probable cause statement.
One of the paintings was spray-painted with black lettering and left near the front entrance, Sinema told authorities.
She also reported finding shards of glass from broken alcohol bottles scattered throughout her house and inside the pool.

Ammel was arrested Sept. 17 after being released from a mental health facility, according to the probable cause document. It was not immediately clear when Ammel entered the facility or why he was admitted.
He was charged with aggravated criminal damage and has been released on his own recognizance. Ammel is due to appear in court in early October. It is not clear whether Ammel has retained a lawyer.

This is not the first time Sinema and Ammel have made headlines. Earlier this month, a North Carolina judge ruled that the former senator could be sued under the state’s “home-wrecker” law over her relationship with Ammel, who was married at the time of their relationship.

North Carolina is one of a handful of states that allow spurned spouses to sue for “alienation of affection” and to seek compensation from a third party responsible for the breakup of their marriage. The law gives aggrieved spouses up to three years to sue. Proceedings are separate from divorces, and jilted spouses must show that the accused “took steps that a reasonable person would expect and did result in the ending of the affectionate marriage between the couple,” according to Cornell Law School.
In 2025, a North Carolina influencer was ordered to pay $1.75 million for destroying her manager’s marriage, WRAL reported.

Sinema acknowledged the affair but argued she has no connection to the state and cannot be sued there. U.S. District Judge David A. Bragdon rejected that argument, pointing to nine text messages she sent Ammel while he was in North Carolina. The judge said the suit can move forward.
The lawsuit, filed by Ammel’s ex-wife, seeks financial damages from Sinema.
According to the complaint, the Ammels had “a good and loving marriage” with “genuine love and affection” before Sinema pursued Matthew Ammel despite knowing he was married.

Matthew Ammel joined Sinema’s security team after retiring from the Army in 2022. He accompanied her on domestic and foreign travel for several years, according to court records, and was later given a position as national security fellow in her Senate office while he continued to work as her bodyguard.

title: Senate rejects resolution calling to end the Iran war, as most Republicans stick with Trump
summary: The Senate voted to direct President Donald Trump to end the U.S. war with Iran, after several Republicans defected and voted with Democrats.
story: WASHINGTON — The Senate on Thursday rejected a symbolic resolution calling for President Donald Trump to end the U.S. war with Iran, with most Republicans siding with the president despite the war’s unpopularity.
Just a handful of Republicans joined Democrats in favor of the resolution: Sens. Rand Paul of Kentucky, Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska and Thom Tillis of North Carolina.

But the majority of the GOP voted against the measure, including Sens. Jon Husted of Ohio and Dan Sullivan of Alaska, who are in some of the most competitive races. Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., was the only Democrat to vote no.
The final vote was 49-50.
Add to Google
Add to Google

The measure passed the House in July by a vote of 214-208. Prices on gas, diesel, fertilizer and food have all risen in the U.S. as Iran has turned the Strait of Hormuz into a war zone in retaliation against military strikes that began in February. Nineteen U.S. service members have died.

A recent NBC News poll found that just 33% of registered voters believe the Iran war was worth it, while 62% believe it was not worth it. By a margin of 57%-24%, voters are more likely to support a candidate who opposes the Iran war.

As a concurrent resolution, the measure expresses the view of Congress. Had it passed the Senate, it would not go to the president for a signature or veto, making it a largely symbolic rebuke of Trump’s ongoing war.

It stated: “Congress hereby directs the President to remove the use of United States Armed Forces from hostilities against the Islamic Republic of Iran or any part of its government or military, including potential ground forces in a combat role or used for occupation, unless explicitly authorized by a declaration of war or specific authorization for use of military force against Iran.”

While most Republicans in both chambers continue to side with Trump on the war, some candidates in competitive 2026 elections have defected amid negative public sentiment. In recent days, GOP Senate candidates like Mike Rogers in Michigan and Rep. Ashley Hinson in Iowa have called for ending the war after siding with Trump on it for months.

“It’s more than a message,” Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., said of the war powers resolution. “Congress has the constitutional power to declare war, not the president. So that’s the reason it doesn’t go to the White House, because the White House can’t veto the Constitution.”
Kaine has led the charge in the Senate to reassert Congress’ power to declare war, hoping to put pressure on Trump.

“If you don’t want to listen to us, how about listen to the American public who’s suffering? Listen to the 18 families who’ve lost loved ones,” Kaine said. “Listen to the hundreds of troops who’ve been injured. Listen to the families, the eight who tried to commit suicide in the extended appointment on the Lincoln.”
Trump has defended the war as an effort to weaken Iran and prevent the country from building a nuclear weapon.

“Just imagine such a vile regime were ever empowered to carry out large-scale terror attacks from behind a nuclear shield. This was the reality we had to confront. A reality that far too many preferred to ignore,” Trump told world leaders in a speech at the United Nations on Wednesday.

title: Iran’s president says Tehran wants a deal with U.S. before midterm elections
summary: Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on Thursday suggested his government was willing to make a deal with the U.S. to end the war before Americans head to the polls this November.
story: Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on Thursday suggested his government was willing to make a deal with the U.S. to end the war before Americans head to the polls this November.
“We don’t want it to get to the midterm elections,” Pezeshkian said Thursday in a brief meeting with NBC News and other news organizations on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly.

“We wish Americans to return to the MOU before the midterms,” Pezeshkian added, referring to a memorandum of understanding between the U.S. and Iran that laid out plans for a temporary ceasefire. The agreement, signed in June, eventually collapsed.

In response to NBC News’ request for comment, White House spokesperson Anna Kelly said: “The Iranian regime has murdered thousands of its own people, killed Americans overseas, executed acts of terrorism in the Strait of Hormuz, and launched indiscriminate attacks against its neighbors in the region.”
“The President is courageously ensuring that such an evil country never possesses a nuclear weapon, which will make the entire world safer and more stable,” Kelly added.

Pezeshkian’s comments came two days after President Donald Trump said in a speech to world leaders at the U.N. that he believed the Iranian regime would not make a deal to settle the conflict until after the fall elections.
“I believe we’ll make a deal right after the election because it doesn’t make sense for them not to,” Trump said. “They’re waiting to see how I do in the midterm election.”

Polls show Democrats with an advantage heading into the November contests. The latest NBC News Decision Desk Poll found 31% of respondents approved of Trump’s handling of the Iran war, while another 69% disapproved.
Trump on Tuesday also defended the conflict and said he was considering whether to “annihilate” the country or make a deal.

Trump has repeatedly said that the goal of attacking Iran was to prevent the development of a nuclear weapon. Soon after the war started, Iran blocked the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway through which some 20% of the world’s oil flowed before the conflict, sending shock waves through the world economy.
In an exchange with news organizations, Pezeshkian said he has met with the Islamic Republic’s new leader twice — including a month ago, for seven hours.

Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei assumed the role in early March after his father, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, was killed in an Israeli attack that also killed family members and other senior leaders.

Pezeshkian said he did not see “any issues with his health or physical appearance” in their meetings, adding that they sat on the floor on traditional pillows. Mojtaba Khamenei was severely injured in the strike that killed his father, three people with knowledge of the matter told NBC News in July, with burns to his face and body and wounds that have required several operations to one of his legs.

Iran’s president briefly addressed other pressing issues affecting the relationship between Tehran and Washington. He said his government was “open” to inspections of its nuclear facilities, which the regime has long maintained is for civilian purposes, and he insisted the regime was not seeking to assassinate the American president.
“This has not been the position of the Iranian government that we seek to assassinate President Trump or his family members,” Pezeshkian said.
The Justice Department last November charged an Iranian man in an alleged murder-for-hire effort to kill Trump when he was the Republican presidential candidate in 2024.
Two others were charged for allegedly planning to kill an Iranian American journalist and activist who has criticized the Iranian government over its treatment of women.

U.S. authorities said the plot was part of Iran’s efforts to avenge the death of a top Iranian general, Qassem Soleimani, who was killed in Baghdad in a U.S. drone strike Trump ordered during his first term in the White House.
Pezeshkian has previously denied an Iranian plot to kill Trump, telling NBC News’ Lester Holt in Tehran last year that the regime would “never” do so.

title: 49ers’ Kyle Juszczyk fined nearly $15K after NFL says he pretended to chug beer on field
summary: The NFL fined San Francisco 49ers fullback Kyle Juszczyk for an alleged act of “offensive demonstration” — when the league says he feigned chugging a brew in the end zone to celebrate a touchdown.
story: The NFL fined San Francisco 49ers fullback Kyle Juszczyk for an alleged act of “offensive demonstration” — when the league says he feigned chugging a brew in the end zone to celebrate a touchdown.
In the third quarter of an eventual 35-13 Niners win over the Miami Dolphins on Sunday, Juszczyk caught a 6-yard scoring toss from Brock Purdy.
Juszczyk embraced teammates Mike Evans and Deebo Samuel before bringing his right hand up to his mouth. Juszczyk tilted his head back, then mimed drinking a pretend liquid.
That celly was deemed to be excessive and unsportsmanlike, leading to a fine of nearly $15,000, ESPN first reported on Thursday.
“Your imitation of chugging a beer constituted an offensive demonstration and could reasonably be construed as being in poor taste,” the NFL wrote in its fine letter, according to ESPN.
Juszczyk then confirmed the report with a bemused re-post on X: “Can’t make this stuff up.”
The 35-year-old  Juszczyk is in his 14th year of pro football and 10th with the Niners.
He’s one of team’s most popular players, with 49ers faithful breaking out into chants of “Juice,” his nickname, every time the Harvard graduate carries or catches the ball.
The 10-time Pro Bowl fullback has also gained fame in recent years through the rising profile of his wife, designer Kristin  Juszczyk. The football fashionista has a line with the NFL.
Representatives for the NFL and 49ers could not be immediately reached for comment on Thursday.

title: St. Paul mayor called herself ‘MILF’ and touched police chief’s thigh, sexual harassment suit claims
summary: The St. Paul, Minnesota, police chief has sued the city’s first female mayor, claiming that she sexually harassed him and “embarked on a campaign” of retaliation after he reported the alleged abuse.
story: The St. Paul, Minnesota, police chief has sued the city’s first female mayor, claiming that she sexually harassed him and “embarked on a campaign” of retaliation after he reported the alleged abuse.

Chief Axel Henry, who has led the St. Paul Police Department since 2022, said Mayor Kaohly Her grabbed “his upper thigh beneath a conference-room table — not once, but twice — during a (St. Paul Police Department) budget meeting.”
Henry, in the lawsuit filed on Wednesday, said Her made sexual innuendos about the size of his penis and described herself to him as a “MILF,” which is an acronym for “mother I’d like to f---.”
Her, according to the lawsuit, also confided in Henry that her own marriage was in trouble and warned the police chief that they “needed to be ‘friends’ or ‘this is not going to work.’”

The 73-page lawsuit filed in Ramsey County District Court, which names Her and the city as defendants, also contains previously reported allegations that the mayor created “a hostile and demeaning environment” for his staff by sending a meme about “good weinering.”
“Wienering” is an internet slang term for sexual intercourse and is frequently misspelled as “weinering.”
Henry is seeking a jury trial to determine damages for “lost wages and benefits, emotional distress, humiliation, and harm to reputation.”
In response to Henry’s lawsuit, Her’s chief spokesperson, Matt Wagenius, released a statement denying the police chief’s major allegations.

“An independent investigation did not substantiate claims of sexual harassment or retaliation against any city employee,” it said. “The Mayor will continue to lead Saint Paul and follow the recommendations of the report. Beyond that, the City of Saint Paul doesn’t comment on active litigation.”
When approached and asked by reporters about the lawsuit’s claims while she was shopping in an Aldi store on Thursday, Her said she cannot comment “because it’s pending litigation.”

That investigation did, however, conclude that Her “engaged in offensive and inappropriate behavior” with her employees. The mayor has issued two apologies and explained that some of her “attempts at humor” fell flat.
Her, who took office in January, has been under fire since July when The Minnesota Star-Tribune first reported that Henry had submitted a sexual harassment complaint against the mayor.

Henry, in the lawsuit, also claims that the mayor hired a private public relations firm to discredit Henry after the investigation got underway. And he alleged that St. Paul city officials violated the Minnesota Whistleblower Act when they “engaged in a series of retaliatory acts” because of the sexual harassment complaint.

The chief also recounted that in December he and the mayor met at a cigar lounge with Todd Hurley, president of the St. Paul Port Authority, to discuss potentially moving the police station downtown to attract more businesses.
Her, according to the lawsuit, allegedly told Henry at that meeting that if she didn’t get her way she would just tell people that Hurley “grabbed her ass.”
“At the time, the comment struck Chief Henry as reflecting a crude sense of humor; he later came to believe that Mayor Her likely had not been joking,” the lawsuit states.
Henry, in the lawsuit, also stated that Her would work out at the gym at police headquarters where she would allegedly make “grunting and moaning noises that sounded like she was having an orgasm.”
Her, according to the lawsuit, also doctored photographs of Henry and other police officers and displayed the “sexualized” images in a gold frame in the chief’s office.

Just days before Henry filed the lawsuit, Her’s office requested that the Ramsey County Sheriff’s Office take over the role of providing security for the mayor from the SPPD, citing “the ongoing threat and increased incidents of political violence towards elected officials.”

Neither the police department nor the sheriff’s office cited Her’s strained relationship with Henry and the St. Paul police department as a reason for the security switch. The sheriff’s office said it was contacted on Sept. 10 to provide security services. The police department said it will “continue monitoring for any threats” against the mayor’s office.
Her, 53, was born in Laos and spent part of her childhood in a refugee camp. She was 3 when she arrived in the U.S., and she grew up in Illinois and Wisconsin, according to her campaign biography.

title: Bodies of 5th grade teacher and student recovered from water after incident during field trip
summary: The bodies of a 5th-grade student and teacher were recovered from the water at Lake MacBride State Park in Iowa following an incident during a field trip.
story: The bodies of a 5th-grade student and teacher were recovered from the water at Lake MacBride State Park in Iowa following an incident during a field trip.
The Johnson County Sheriff’s Office was called to the park Tuesday afternoon for reports of people in the water near Coralville Reservoir, a news release states.
The body of Hannah Jorgensen, 24, of Tiffin, was pulled from the water around 12:43 p.m., and a search was launched for a missing 10-year-old boy.
The child, Ahmed Osman, of Iowa City, was found dead Wednesday, authorities said in an update.
Fifth-grade students from Borlaug Elementary School were on a “School of the Wild Field Trip,” NBC affiliate KWWL of Waterloo, Iowa, reported.
Iowa City Community School District confirmed the deaths in a Facebook post on Thursday.

“Our hearts are shattered by the loss of two beloved members of our Borlaug Elementary family, fifth-grade teacher Hannah Jorgensen and fifth-grade student Ahmed Osman. There are simply no words that can adequately express the depth of this loss,” the district said.

“Hannah and Ahmed were so much more than members of our school community. They were a teacher and student, a colleague and classmate, a friend, and most importantly, deeply loved members of their families.”
The district said “their absence will be felt in the classrooms and hallways of Borlaug, in the lives of those who loved them, and throughout our entire school district community.”
“We will remember Hannah. We will remember Ahmed. And we will carry their memory with us,” the statement read.
Norman Borlaug Elementary School thanked the community for its support.

“Our building is hurting right now, and so are our hearts. But knowing that you are all here for us, standing beside us, checking in, and, lifting us up. It means more than we can put into words,” the school said.
The sheriff’s office said the incident remains under investigation.

title: Elizabeth Holmes to be transferred to a halfway house
summary: Holmes, 42, was sentenced to more than 11 years in prison for defrauding investors of millions of dollars through Theranos, the failed blood-testing company that she founded.
story: Elizabeth Holmes, who was convicted of fraud for siphoning  hundreds of millions of dollars from several high-profile investors, is scheduled to be transferred from a minimum-security federal prison to a halfway house next year, according to one of her victims.

Holmes, 42, defrauded investors of millions through Theranos, the failed blood-testing company that she founded. She was sentenced in 2022 to 11 years and three months in prison. She and her business partner Ramesh “Sunny” Balwani were ordered to pay 12 victims a total of $452 million in restitution.
Holmes has been serving that sentence at a minimum-security prison in Bryan, Texas. The halfway house will provide her greater freedom.
Alan Eisenman, one of her victims, said she is to be transferred to the Austin Transitional Center, a halfway house in Del Valle, an unincorporated community that borders Austin, Texas.
The Department of Justice is required by law to notify victims of crime of case developments through letters and emails.

Scott Taylor, a spokesperson for the Bureau of Prisons, said he could not provide details of Holmes’ confinement, including release plans. Taylor cited safety, security and a Bureau of Prisons policy that says such information can’t be released until after an individual arrives at their designated institution.

Eisenman, an early Theranos investor who testified at Holmes’ trial, said he received a message from the Justice Department’s victim notification system Wednesday saying the halfway house transfer would occur in August 2027.

Eisenman, a retired financial planner from Texas, invested about $1.2 million with his family in the failed blood-testing company beginning in 2006. He was the smallest investor among a list of high-profile, well-monied investors who included Australian media mogul Rupert Murdoch.
Eisenman was unhappy to hear of the planned transfer.
“Seems like a gift,” he told NBC News.
Holmes owes Eisenman and his wife, Sherrie, almost $150,000 out of a total of $452 million in restitution for all victims of her crimes, according to a court document.
So far, he has “not received a penny” from Holmves, he told NBC News.
“She was a liar back in 2006,” Eisenman said, “and she’s a liar today.”
Eisenman said he hoped Holmes would remain in prison through her scheduled release date of Feb. 22, 2030, after some reductions in the sentence.

In March, a judge cut Holmes’ sentence from 135 months to 123 months. According to a court document, the judge agreed with Holmes that she did not personally cause “substantial financial hardship” to her victims.

The government had tried to prevent a reduction of her prison time, arguing that Holmes has not accepted responsibility for her crimes, paid minimal restitution and “has the opportunity to reoffend,” according to a court filing.

The government told the court that Holmes has continued to tell national media she intends to resume a career in healthcare technology after her release and has been advising her romantic partner on fundraising for his startup, a company that has similarities to Theranos, the court document states.
Eisenman added that he’s against Holmes receiving any form of presidential clemency. She filed for a commutation of her sentence last year. It remains pending.
Holmes’ attorney from her trial did not respond to a phone message from NBC News requesting comment. ABC News first reported her pending release to the halfway house.
Walter Pavlo, president of Prisonology LLC consulting firm, said a combination of factors could have helped reduce the time Holmes is spending in prison and at the halfway house.

Those include a change on sentencing guidelines, good conduct time, possible participation in programs that slice time off her sentence if successfully completed and laws governing time she would spend in a halfway house and home confinement.
Pavlo said inmates who report to halfway houses can work, have a phone and drive to religious services or shop for things they need and can earn passes for weekends at home.
On its website, the Bureau of Prisons states that inmates at halfway houses are given counseling, job placement and other programs and services to help rebuild community ties.

The BOP site states it monitors inmates’ activities, requires sign out and conducts head counts. Also, inmates “ordinarily” are expected to work 40 hours a week within 15 days of their arrival at the halfway house and some of their income pay for some of their stay at the halfway house, according to the BOP site.
The news of Holmes’ impending move comes as a documentary about her is about to be released.

The documentary by comedian Nathan Fielder and director Lance Oppenheim is based on Fielder living with her and her partner for several days before she entered prison in 2023. It recently made its debut at the Telluride Film Festival and is scheduled for full release next month.
Eisenman said he also watched the latest trailer for the documentary, “You Can See Everything,” and plans to see it upon its release next month.
His concern, he added, is whether it will portray Holmes as a sympathetic figure.
“She’s obviously manipulative,” Eisenman said. “If people don’t see that, then they’re blind. She’s the most conniving person I’ve ever met.”

title: Macklemore announces Free Palestine Tour
summary: Macklemore announced he will launch the Free Palestine Tour this fall after being removed from Ed Sheeran’s tour this month over his pro-Palestinian performance.
story: Macklemore announced he will launch the Free Palestine Tour this fall after being removed from Ed Sheeran’s tour this month over his pro-Palestinian performance.
The “Thrift Shop” rapper took to Instagram on Monday and jokingly said that his “schedule freed up a bit,” announcing three performance dates in Dublin, London and Paris next month.

“What happened to me is bigger than one artist or one stage,” he wrote. “When the billionaire class can decide which voices are allowed on stage and which ones are too dangerous to hear, everyone should be paying attention.”

The performances are part of what Macklemore named the “Free Palestine” tour and the poster said it would be him “and friends.” He said he spent the last week reaching out to other artists to work out scheduling, but no other names have been announced as of Monday.
He wrote that there has been a “been a collective awakening around Palestinian liberation” and the expectations of artists.
“It’s 2026. Being apolitical during a genocide doesn’t work anymore,” Macklemore said. “People are asking artists to show up, educate themselves and be in community.”
All proceeds from the performances would benefit organizations supporting Palestinians, he said.
Robert Kraft intervenes

Macklemore, whose real name is Ben Haggerty, announced earlier this month that U.S. venues gave Sheeran an ultimatum to remove him from the tour or face show cancelations. Macklemore said that New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft “rallied” other stadium owners after taking issue with his “Free Palestine” remarks during a show.
Sheeran confirmed that Kraft was among those who called him after Macklemore performed his anti-war song and the speech that preceded it at Metlife Stadium circulated online.

The situation surrounding Macklemore, Sheeran and Kraft made international headlines this month as many debated not just Macklemore’s speech regarding the Israel-Gaza war, but also the rights for artists to express their views.

It began when Macklemore joined Sheeran’s “Loop” tour in New Jersey and performed “Hind’s Hall,” his song inspired by the anti-war protests at Columbia University in 2024. Macklemore made a speech prior to the performance that called for a “Free Palestine” and also told Jewish members of the audience that his comments regarding the Israeli government was in no way about them. The performance of “Hind’s Hall” also had related images from pro-Palestinian demonstrations and the situation in Gaza.

Kraft did not deny allegations made by Macklemore in his own statement earlier this month, but said Gillette Stadium — which his entertainment group owns — seeks to create a welcoming environment for everyone. He took issue with Macklemore’s actions at the New Jersey show and “and a broader history of antisemitic rhetoric and imagery that we believe has been deeply offensive and hurtful to the Jewish community.”

“Much of my time and attention for the last decade has been focused on the fight against antisemitism and hate of all kinds, and I feel a responsibility to stand up when I believe that line has been crossed,” Kraft said.
The Patriots owner also said he was not trying to stifle Palestinian advocacy or diminish the suffering of Palestinians.

Kraft did not specifically reference past actions of concern from Macklemore, but many online brought up a 2014 incident in which Macklemore wore a costume that appeared to play on antisemitic tropes: a wig, a fake beard and a hooked nose. He wore it to the Grammys that year, saying at the time that he thought it would be fun to dress in disguise to talk to fans.

Macklemore apologized after the antisemitic stereotype was pointed out, saying he had been in touch with the Anti-Defamation League, an organization founded to combat antisemitism. The ADL accepted the apology at the time, saying it took him “at his word that he did not have any ill intent,” according to The Guardian.
Ed Sheeran backlash

Sheeran faced a wave of backlash over his role in the situation as some commenters felt that the singer should have taken a stance on the war or at least Macklemore’s right to speak on his opinion. All of Sheeran’s opening acts, as well as his house band, dropped out of their scheduled U.S. tour dates in solidarity with Macklemore and the Palestinian people.

The “Perfect” singer initially released a statement explaining his side of the situation and clarifying that it was not his choice to drop Macklemore. Sheeran said that his promoters, who held the contract with Macklemore, made the decision as he attempted to build bridges with venue owners.
Sheeran went on with his scheduled concert in Philadelphia on Saturday, tearfully addressing the crowd who showed up in spite of the criticism he faced.

“I’ve never wanted to be an activist musician,” Sheeran said. “But this has put me in the middle of an important and passionate argument about freedom of speech and the most complex political issue on the planet.”

Israel launched its offensive in the Gaza Strip after the Hamas-led attacks on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and roughly 250 others were taken hostage. More than 73,000 people have been killed in Gaza during Israel’s military campaign, including at least 1,200 since a fragile ceasefire took effect in October, according to the Palestinian Health Ministry.

Sheeran acknowledged the “horrific” Oct. 7 attack on Israel by Hamas which started the war, but went on to say what has happened in Gaza as a result is “catastrophic and unjustifiable and disproportionate.”
“This is a humanitarian issue and I cannot hide how I feel about it anymore,” he said.

title: Dee Brock, original director of the Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders, dies at age 96
summary: Dee Brock, the original director of the Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders who helped mold the prototype for NFL sideline entertainment, died on Wednesday, the team said.
story: Dee Brock, the original director of the Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders who helped mold the prototype for NFL sideline entertainment, died on Wednesday, the team said.
She was 96.
Former Cowboys cheerleader Kelli Finglass – now the team’s director – called Brock a “visionary who helped create an icon.”

“Dee’s leadership, imagination and unwavering commitment to excellence shaped far more than a team. She created a standard, a spirit and a symbol that have inspired generations and earned recognition around the world,” Finglass said in a statement.

“Her influence lives on in every performance, every dream pursued and every woman who has ever worn the uniform with pride. We are deeply grateful for her vision, her courage and the extraordinary legacy she leaves with the Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders.”
Finglass added: “Rest peacefully, Dee. You will always be remembered and your legacy will continue to shine.”
When the squad was first formed in 1961, Brock according to the team’s history, “utilized high school students with traditional cheers to lead the crowd.”

The team added “dance elements” to its game-day routine in 1965, then in 1972 introduced its now-iconic uniforms — boots, short shorts and a fringed, midriff bearing top — which has remained virtually unchanged since.
Brock retired in 1975.
The team honored Brock in 2022 with a lifetime achievement award, presented as a rhinestone-adorned football.
“I hadn’t realized I had made such a good impression, and I’m so happy about that,” Brock told NBC affiliate KETK during the presentation ceremony at her Tyler home.
Brock’s advocacy is credited with helping integrate the cheerleading squad.

“The kindness that she showed, the encouragement, the warmth to a 16-year-old high school girl, it’s amazing what encouraging words, what kindness can do.” said Eunice Cicero, a pioneering member of the 1965 squad. “Thanks to Dee, I had the pleasure of being one of the first African American cheerleaders for the Dallas Cowboys.”
